item.title: Enhancing Democratic Listening in Online Discussions: The Role of Reaction Buttons, Discussion Moderation, and Large Language Models
item.dc:creator: Shota Gelovani, Philipp Müller, Hartmut Weßler, Hendrik Meyer, Louisa Pröschel, Anke Stoll, Marc Ziegele
item.description:
Political Communication · Shota Gelovani, Philipp Müller, Hartmut Weßler, Hendrik Meyer, Louisa Pröschel, Anke Stoll, Marc Ziegele

Topics: Democratic listening, Online discussion, Large Language Models, Content moderation

Political communication research in general – and research on political online discussions in particular – has previously focused on the exercise of democratic voice and thus largely neglected the complementary practice of democratic listening. Against the backdrop of a wide-spread perception that democratic listening is lacking in online discussions, we investigate whether listening can be strengthened through novel platform affordances. We developed an experimental online written discussion platform with listening-oriented reaction buttons and both human and AI moderation (based on GPT-4). We then conducted an experiment involving n = 740 respondents in 40 discussion groups (N = 4,355 comments), each lasting 30 minutes, covering three experimental conditions and a control condition. We compare the effect of (1) listening-oriented reaction buttons versus (2) a combination of these buttons and listening-oriented human discussion moderation versus (3) a combination of buttons and AI moderation on the level of democratic listening demonstrated in discussants’ textual contributions. We find that listening-oriented buttons alone do not enhance democratic listening. However, when combined with listening-oriented AI moderation, they are associated with a democratic listening rate of 27% within discussions, compared to 21% in the condition without either feature. Our findings lay the basis for the implementation of a combination of listening-oriented buttons and discussion moderation on news media websites, social media apps or dedicated discussion spaces using LLM-based chatbots.

item.title: How does young children’s digital resilience operate within and across homes and communities? A thematic analysis of parents and early years educators’ experiences
item.dc:creator: Simon P. Hammond, Jeanette D’Arcy, Laura Jennings-Tallent, Gray Prothero-Gibbs, Sandra El Gemayel, Harry T. Dyer
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Simon P. Hammond, Jeanette D’Arcy, Laura Jennings-Tallent, Gray Prothero-Gibbs, Sandra El Gemayel, Harry T. Dyer

Topics: Digital resilience, Social capital, Parental mediation, Qualitative methods

This paper examines how young children aged 0–5 years build digital resilience within interconnected home and community contexts. While playing, exploring, and socialising are central to early experiential learning, little is known about how parents/carers and educators support children to recognise, manage, and recover from mistakes in connected environments. Conceptualising digital resilience as a socio-ecological construct, the paper draws on findings from the TYKES project to address this gap. Using a multi-method qualitative design, the study thematically analyses semi-structured interviews with parents/carers (n = 17) and early years educators (n = 5), alongside focus groups with educators across two settings (n = 8), conducted using purposive sampling over a ten-month period (May 2024–February 2025). The paper argues that digital resilience is a relational and context-dependent process that unfolds across nested home and community environments, rather than solely within individual children or discrete settings. It highlights the importance of social capital and everyday interactions in shaping children’s emerging capacities to navigate online challenges. The paper contributes to the literature by demonstrating how parents/carers and educators actively cultivate digital resilience as an emergent capability, embedded in socio-ecological relations. The findings point to the need for more holistic and coordinated support across education systems, policymakers, industry, and governments to enable young children to thrive on the Internet.

item.title: Black technofeminism as critique of biological essentialism in AI anthropomorphization
item.dc:creator: Melissa C. Brown
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Melissa C. Brown

Topics: Artificial intelligence, Intersectionality, Generative AI, Gender representation

This article uses Black technofeminism to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) anthropomorphization coincides with racialized and gendered dehumanization. It builds on Black feminist thought to inform a qualitative audit of YouTube search media and images generated by Gemini and ChatGPT as a discourse on AI and humanity. The findings reveal how humans associated with AI are predominantly portrayed as white men, while AI entities are typically embodied as white women. In contrast, Black women are notably absent from general AI search results yet are disproportionately depicted as AI-generated entities portrayed in dehumanizing ways. Images of women generated by the multimodal large language models (MLLMs) default to whiteness. Because the models require a racial identifier in the prompt to show Black women, both MLLMs distort their features, including favoring lighter skin and looser hair textures as ‘more feminine.’ I argue that AI visual culture reinforces hierarchical power relations by embedding biologically deterministic constructs of humanity, rooted in racial and gender essentialism, into digital environments. It therefore concludes that Black technofeminism resituates understandings of intersectionality in the study of racial and gender bias as a critique of power, revealing AI's paradoxical implementation as a tool of progress and an instrument of oppression.

item.title: War, Feelings of Belonging, and News Diets: How Russia’s Full-Scale Invasion of Ukraine Did (Not) Change the News Repertoires of Russian Speakers in Germany
item.dc:creator: Anna Ryzhova, Eunike Piwoni, Florian Toepfl
item.description:
Digital Journalism · Anna Ryzhova, Eunike Piwoni, Florian Toepfl

Topics: News consumption, Media use, Social media, Disinformation

This study examines how Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, launched in February 2022, has influenced the news repertoires of first-generation Russian-speaking migrants living in Germany. While previous research suggests that news consumption patterns are typically stable, it has also shown that major disruptive events - such as the COVID-19 pandemic - have the potential for significant shifts. However, little research has explored how wars impact the transnational news repertoires of migrant communities. Grounded in 25 semi-structured interviews, the study demonstrates that the four types of news repertoires identified by previous research on Russian speakers in Germany prior to 2022 remained valid. Although very few participants indicated that they had completely switched repertoire type, nuanced changes were observed within the four types. These changes were accompanied by a complex process of renegotiating their sense of belonging to Russia. Moreover, across the four types, there was a spike in news use in the first weeks of the full-scale war, followed by news avoidance, and a “migration” to the platform Telegram. This study advances research on diasporic news repertoires, digital war, and disinformation by showing that geopolitical crises can shape the news repertoires of transnational audiences who have feelings of belonging to actors involved in conflict.

item.title: Negotiating Infrastructural Integration: Cloud Services and the Evolution of News Website Ecosystems in France and the Netherlands
item.dc:creator: Agustin Ferrari Braun, Fernando van der Vlist, Thomas Poell
item.description:
Digital Journalism · Agustin Ferrari Braun, Fernando van der Vlist, Thomas Poell

Topics: Digital platforms, Journalism, Digital journalism, Digital media

This paper analyzes the infrastructural integration of European news media with digital platforms and third-party service providers between 2015–2025. Reviewing current research, we note increased scholarly attention to the infrastructural relations between news organizations and digital platforms. Yet, despite this heightened interest, we are still missing a systematic empirical examination of how infrastructural integration shapes the spaces of negotiation between news media and tech companies. We provide such an examination through a historical analysis of the top ten news websites in France and the Netherlands, using a custom version of the 4CAT Capture and Analysis Toolkit on 9,456 archived snapshots. The analysis of evolving third-party service (de-)integrations, highlight the rise of audiovisual content and the decline of website analytics, as well as broader industry and regulatory developments (e.g., GDPR). These changes in website architectures point to shifting strategies of news organizations to adapt and preserve their independence in an online environment increasingly dominated by digital platforms. Yet, paradoxically, those strategies are enabled by cloud infrastructures provided by the same platform companies, deepening the dependence of news organizations on these companies. Thus, infrastructural integration is a process of demarcation of spaces and activities between news organizations and tech companies.

item.title: Calls to action and voter engagement on Facebook: a comparative study of eight European election campaigns
item.dc:creator: Anders Olof Larsson, Daniel N. Jackson, Márton Bene, Andreu Casero-Ripollés, Vicente Fenoll, Dren Gërguri, Jörg Haßler, Simon Kruschinski, Sara Monteiro Machado, Alena Macková
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Anders Olof Larsson, Daniel N. Jackson, Márton Bene, Andreu Casero-Ripollés, Vicente Fenoll, Dren Gërguri, Jörg Haßler, Simon Kruschinski, Sara Monteiro Machado, Alena Macková

Topics: Political communication, Social media, Political engagement, Election campaigns

This study examines the use of Facebook by political actors across eight European countries – Czech Republic, Germany, Hungary, Kosovo, Norway, Portugal, Spain, United Kingdom – as they attempt to engage voters through calls to action. By analysing what is often referred to as the supply and demand of political communication, the paper conceptualizes three primary types of calls to action: informing, mobilizing, and interacting. Our findings reveal that mobilizing calls are the most prevalent, reflecting the central mission of election campaigns to secure voter turnout. However, such calls do not necessarily result in higher user engagement compared to informative content. Despite the potential for interactive features to enhance dialogic communication, they remain underutilized, with political actors apparently favouring controlled interactivity to maintain message control. The study highlights significant cross-country differences, with variations in the degree of engagement reached by different calls to action as influenced by national political contexts and campaign cultures. The research underscores the importance of considering both the strategic priorities of political actors and the cultural and institutional factors that shape voter engagement on social media.

item.title: Data visualisation as an ‘emotional repository’
item.dc:creator: Monika Frątczak
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Monika Frątczak

Topics: Data visualisation, Climate change communication, Social media, Emotion regulation

Understanding the role of emotions in engagements with data visualisations (graphs, charts, maps) is important given their increasing circulation in everyday life and their influence on how people make sense of social and political issues. This paper builds on sociological perspectives on emotions and advances existing research on the interplay between data visualisation and emotions by proposing the concept of ‘emotional repository’ to describe data visualisations. I argue that data visualisations do not simply evoke emotional responses but become sites where emotions attach to, accumulate around, and acquire meaning through specific visual, data, and socio-political contexts. To explore this, the paper draws on empirical research, analysing thirty-four semi-structured interviews and thirteen follow-up interviews with diverse social media users who responded to climate data visualisations published on social media by environmental organisations. The paper makes an original contribution to the limited existing research on data visualisation in society by showing how data visualisations are socially and politically structured through their embedding within broader socio-political contexts. Moreover, it argues that data visualisations have the potential to make distressing topics, such as climate disaster, more palatable and aesthetically enjoyable, thereby influencing how social media users emotionally engage with and respond to the information presented in the data visualisation. The findings suggest that approaches to data visualisation should extend beyond clarity and accuracy to consider the social, political, and emotional contexts that shape how people engage with data.

item.title: Building and Maintaining Trust in AI Chatbots: Introducing Generative Information Retrieval Accountability Assessment Framework (GIRAAF)
item.dc:creator: Michael Karlsson, Joanne Kuai, Cornelia Brantner, Haiqing Yu, James Meese
item.description:
Journal of Broadcasting & Electronic Media · Michael Karlsson, Joanne Kuai, Cornelia Brantner, Haiqing Yu, James Meese

Topics: Artificial intelligence, Large Language Models, Trust, Algorithmic accountability

Social integration of AI requires public trust and appropriate governance. This paper introduces the Generative Information Retrieval Accountability Assessment Framework (GIRAAF), designed to appraise accountability for Large Language Models and their applications, including AI chatbots. Drawing on Dahl’s (1998) notion of enlightened citizens, the framework comprises six interlinked dimensions: Information Readiness, Factual Correctness, Normative Alignment, Sourcing Practice, Transparency and Explainability, and Responsiveness and Adaptivity. Together, these dimensions link observable text outputs to intelligible standards, enabling systematic evaluation and accountable oversight. For scholars, developers and policymakers, GIRAAF provides a diagnostic heuristic and shared vocabulary for critical analysis of AI chatbot performance.

item.title: DIMS: a no-code dashboard linking multimodal dynamic signals to communication practices
item.dc:creator: Grace Qiyuan Miao, Michał Weiss, Yuqian Ni, Jingjing Han
item.description:
Communication Methods and Measures · Grace Qiyuan Miao, Michał Weiss, Yuqian Ni, Jingjing Han

Topics: Interpersonal communication, Multimodal analysis, Physiological measurement, Communication research

Communication research increasingly relies on multimodal time-series data spanning physiological, behavioral, audiovisual, and transcript-based measures. Yet the phenomena these data are meant to capture, such as social connection or attitude, often unfold in temporally specific ways that are lost when signals are reduced to averages or analyzed in isolation. This article introduces the Dynamic Interaction and Multimodal Signals (DIMS) Dashboard, an open-source tool that aligns multiple time series with synchronized video and transcript, allowing researchers to inspect how statistically identified patterns correspond to communicative events. We present two exploratory case studies. The first examines inter-brain synchrony during interpersonal conversation; using a dynamic dyadic systems lens, we show how synchrony peaks can be read as candidate dyadic events whose meaning depends on interactional context. The second examines coupled facial electromyography during advertisement viewing; using an emotional-flow lens, we show how orbicularis oculi activity that appears positive in isolation can signal a sustained, co-active mixed-emotion state when paired with corrugator activity. Across both cases, DIMS supports an iterative qualitative-quantitative workflow: quantitative signals flag moments worth inspecting, and qualitative interpretation clarifies what they mean. DIMS does not replace statistical or qualitative analysis but creates a shared analytical space for theoretically meaningful observation.

item.title: OSINV vs. Core International Crimes: Practices and Professional Identities of Ukrainian Journalists, Investigators, and Researchers Investigating Atrocities
item.dc:creator: Johana Kotišová, Dariya Orlova
item.description:
Digital Journalism · Johana Kotišová, Dariya Orlova

Topics: Investigative journalism, Journalistic practice, Professional identity, Digital trace data

In this article, we examine how the practices, technologies, and collaborations of Ukrainian journalists, investigators, and researchers investigating war crimes during the Russo-Ukrainian war—particularly the use of OSINV and their engagement with international legal discourse—shape their professional identities. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork in Ukraine, including semi-structured interviews with 18 professionals investigating war crimes, we ask: How do journalists, investigators, and researchers use OSINV practices and technologies to investigate core international crimes? How do they (re)negotiate their relationships with legal and criminal discourses and institutions? How do journalists, investigators, and researchers investigating core international crimes integrate OSINV practices into their professional identities? Through illustrating how their professional identities absorb OSINV-related practices in the context of armed conflicts, we argue that OSINV-driven atrocity crime investigations lie at multiple intersections of diverse logics, roles, and ways of positioning, particularly the public service logic and the commercial, gamified logic of journalism, the watchdog and the facilitator roles, local and global justice processes, and across the discursive institutions of journalism, law, and human rights. The findings testify to the increasing hybridization of journalism and human rights advocacy, and blur the boundary between storytelling and processes that lead to legal justice.

item.title: Religious information repertoires in Switzerland’s hybrid information environment: asymmetric associations with trust and reputation
item.dc:creator: Rebekka Rieser, Mark Eisenegger
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Rebekka Rieser, Mark Eisenegger

Topics: Media use, Social media, Trust, Digital media

In hybrid media environments, public understanding emerges from patterned combinations of legacy news media, digital platforms, and interpersonal communication. Rather than relying on single channels, individuals assemble repertoires of mediated sources, interpersonal encounters, and direct personal experiences that structure how they make sense of public issues and evaluate social groups. Religion provides an instructive case: as a morally charged and contested domain, it circulates across hybrid media environments while also being shaped by biographical and interpersonal experience. Drawing on a Swiss online survey conducted in 2024 (N = 1,000), we use latent class analysis (LCA) to identify six religious information repertoires based on patterns of digital media use, legacy news consumption, and interpersonal experience. These repertoires are associated with distinct patterns of trust and reputation across Christianity, Islam, Judaism, Hinduism, and Buddhism. Overall, this study advances research on hybrid media environments by showing that combinations of various sources function as infrastructures of public evaluation. The findings indicate that legacy news media and interpersonal experience remain central, while digital-born sources play a more selective role. The study refines repertoire theory and illustrates how everyday information behavior is associated with social recognition and mistrust, with implications for the social-relational foundations of cohesion in pluralistic societies.

item.title: Navigating GenAI in the workplace: skills transformation & tension
item.dc:creator: Simin Michelle Chen, Kate J. Cassidy
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Simin Michelle Chen, Kate J. Cassidy

Topics: Generative AI, Artificial intelligence in journalism, Technology adoption, Digital transformation

By automating the content creation process, Generative AI is reshaping creative work, but its impact on knowledge workers remains underexplored, which this study seeks to examine. Drawing on in-depth interviews with 20 knowledge workers, this study examines what is being transformed in the workplace and how these shifts are being perceived by the knowledge workers who use GenAI. Using Social Shaping of Technology (SST) as a conceptual lens to understand the interaction between technology and knowledge workers, the study finds that participants perceived GenAI as an efficient tool that provides cognitive relief and enhances productivity during times of resource constraint. Tensions also arose around authenticity, creativity, a sense of fulfillment, and the perception of effort. The adoption of GenAI has created downstream labor and demand for new skills as it shifts knowledge workers’ roles away from creator to editor/fact-checker while creating tension as participants balance their desire for efficiency with fears of diminished creativity and domain knowledge, skills atrophy, and threats to content ownership.

item.title: Where the World Connects: How Intergroup Contact on Social Media Influences Intergroup Outcomes
item.dc:creator: Yansheng Liu, Yilan Guo, Alex Thomas Paloma, Mary Beth Oliver
item.description:
Media Psychology · Yansheng Liu, Yilan Guo, Alex Thomas Paloma, Mary Beth Oliver

Topics: Social media, Social identity, Intergroup contact, Computer-mediated communication

This study examines how, following the U.S. TikTok ban and the subsequent digital migration of foreign users to the Chinese social media platform RedNote, mediated intergroup contact with American users shaped intergroup outcomes among Chinese users. Guided by intergroup contact theory and communication accommodation theory, we did two 2 (poster identity: American–outgroup vs. Chinese–ingroup) × 3 (post language: English vs. Chinese vs. both) between-subjects online experiments with Chinese RedNote users (N = 833 in total; Nstudy 1 = 364, Nstudy 2 = 469) to explore how intergroup contact through posts featuring cat images (Study 1) and messages seeking connection (Study 2) influenced intergroup outcomes. Results showed that intergroup contact increased Chinese users’ inclusion of Americans in the self, moral regard toward Americans, and intention to interact with Americans. Such effects were mediated by perceived connectedness with Americans. However, these effects did not extend to broader outgroups—people all over the world. Post language did not play an important role in the process of intergroup contact on social media. Theoretical and practical implications are discussed.

item.title: Individual Political Attitudes and Group Norms Interact to Explain Biased Political Information Sharing
item.dc:creator: Xinyao Zhang, Christin Scholz, Gijs Schumacher, Marte Otten
item.description:
Media Psychology · Xinyao Zhang, Christin Scholz, Gijs Schumacher, Marte Otten

Topics: Political polarization, Social influence, Social norms, Social media use

Previous research shows that people selectively share messages congruent with their political beliefs (pro-attitudinal sharing) and with like-minded others (ingroup sharing). However, it is difficult to observe how characteristics of both individual- and audience-level affect sharing decisions interactively. We address this gap by taking a cross-level, experimental approach. We recruited an online sample of Dutch residents across the political spectrum via a data panel company. Participants were introduced to 4 groups in political-themed group chats. Groups differed in political attitude (left/right) and tolerance to dissent (tolerant/punitive). Per group, participants indicated sharing intention for 4 political messages varying in their alignment with left/right-leaning political ideology. Our pilot (N = 402) and pre-registered, confirmatory main (N = 930) studies found a strong pro-attitudinal sharing effect and, to a lesser extent, ingroup sharing and pro-group sharing. Tolerant group norms increased online sharing in general, regardless of whether the message aligned with the sharer’s individual political attitude. Our findings provide causal evidence of how individual- and group-level factors affect sharing intentions of political information concurrently, and the role of tolerant general group norms to de-bias and promote online sharing. Insights taking into account both individual and group-level factors are thus required to effectively de-bias online political information sharing.

item.title: More Than Core and Periphery: How a Mapping Approach Can Add Nuance to Understanding the Journalistic Field
item.dc:creator: Phoebe Maares, Kim Löhmann, Folker Hanusch, Daniel Nölleke
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Phoebe Maares, Kim Löhmann, Folker Hanusch, Daniel Nölleke

Topics: Journalistic practice, Digital journalism, Journalistic roles, News organizations

The influx of new (digital) actors and the resulting changes to the composition of the journalistic field have attracted considerable attention from journalism scholarship in recent years. However, much of the discussion about the new, so-called peripheral actors and the traditional mainstream has tended to, somewhat simplistically, assume a certain homogeneity in each. Recently, scholarship has begun to question this dichotomy, pointing to the vast variety of peripheral actors as well as traditional journalists, and instead argued for a more relational spectrum along which to locate all actors in the field. Yet, we still have an incomplete, and, crucially, under-theorized understanding of the different kinds of constellations in which peripheral journalism may exist vis-à-vis the so-called core of the journalistic field. To address this research gap, we draw on photo elicitation mappings of 101 journalistic and journalism-like actors in Austria and relate them to their position in the journalistic field. The findings show that both the core and the periphery are more nuanced, yet there are commonalities in their relational position-taking, which adds to our understanding of the journalistic field’s changing boundaries.

item.title: Love Without Borders: Explaining Why People Interact with National Out-Groups on Tinder
item.dc:creator: Ainhoa Arranz Aldana, Giulia Ranzini, Philipp K. Masur
item.description:
Media Psychology · Ainhoa Arranz Aldana, Giulia Ranzini, Philipp K. Masur

Topics: Online dating, Intergroup contact, Social norms, Social identity

Despite our tendency to select romantic partners who are similar to us, a growing body of research seems to suggest that online dating may increase the diversity of couples. However, to this day, there is no clarity around what might drive users to cross social boundaries on these platforms. Building on the Theory of Reasoned Action, we propose a model that integrates individual (e.g. attitudes, perceived norms), relational (e.g. intergroup contact, social identity), and platform-specific antecedents (e.g. use motivation, experience) that could explain national-identity-based intergroup interactions on Tinder. Based on a survey with 668 adult Tinder users living in the Netherlands and the UK, recruited through an online panel, we found that norms and attitudes both positively related to intentions to date national out-groups, which was in turn associated with behavior. Intergroup contact positively relates to intergroup dating norms and, in turn, intergroup dating intentions. The strength of social identity and different motives for using Tinder did not influence intentions. Frequent Tinder usage was linked to greater out-group dating intentions, suggesting online dating could lead to more diverse relationships regarding nationality. Findings highlight the role of intergroup contact and social norms in digital romantic settings.

item.title: Negotiated Adaptability: How Peripheral Actors’ Perceptions of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) Shape Journalistic Practice
item.dc:creator: Kevin C. Mudavadi, Bingbing Zhang, Melissa Tully, Brian Ekdale, Jonas Nyabor, Nur Hossain, Shitemi Khamadi
item.description:
Digital Journalism · Kevin C. Mudavadi, Bingbing Zhang, Melissa Tully, Brian Ekdale, Jonas Nyabor, Nur Hossain, Shitemi Khamadi

Topics: Artificial intelligence in journalism, Generative AI, Journalistic practice, News production

While Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly transforming newsroom practices globally, studies often examine journalists and peripheral actors in isolation, overlooking the reciprocal influence these actors exert on journalism. This study addresses this gap by drawing on 94 semi-structured, in-depth interviews with journalists and peripheral actors in Kenya’s urban and rural areas. Specifically, we examine how Kenyan journalists and peripheral actors engage with GenAI, how they believe it should be used in newsrooms, and how their practices and perspectives shape journalistic adaptation. Our findings show that the adoption of and resistance to GenAI by Kenyan journalists illustrate “negotiated adaptability”—a form of technological adaptation in which journalists’ decisions about whether, where, and how to use GenAI are shaped through ongoing negotiations, including with actors located at the periphery of the newsroom ecosystem.

item.title: From Institutionalized Data to Inconsistent Practices: The Dynamics of Datafied Employee Evaluation in Journalistic Work
item.dc:creator: Rasa Jämsen, Ward van Zoonen, Mikko Villi
item.description:
Digital Journalism · Rasa Jämsen, Ward van Zoonen, Mikko Villi

Topics: Datafication, Journalism, Digital journalism, Journalistic practice

Organizations are increasingly relying on data to evaluate work, yet the role of data in shaping managerial practices remains uneven. The quantitative turn, referred to as datafication, has been an integral part of journalistic organizations for decades, while continuing to raise fundamental challenges for management. This paper examines how datafication is perceived when evaluating and being evaluated through data. Drawing on 25 interviews and 61 open-ended survey responses from a public-service media organization, we show how data becomes institutionalized in everyday work through organizational routines, technologies, and discourses that render data ‘taken-for-granted’. At the same time, its enactment in managerial practices remains uneven. Despite shared access to analytics, managers diverge in how they incorporate data into evaluation and feedback, resulting in inconsistent practices in the same organization. These findings refine research on datafication by demonstrating that institutionalization is selective rather than uniform, and by showing that data-related relational activities within organizations are central to how analytics are interpreted, negotiated, and enacted in practice.

item.title: Mapping Gaps in Local News Coverage
item.dc:creator: Alexander L. Curry, Yujin Kim, Caroline Murray, Emily Graham, Natalie Jomini Stroud
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Alexander L. Curry, Yujin Kim, Caroline Murray, Emily Graham, Natalie Jomini Stroud

Topics: Local news, News coverage, Journalism, Digital media

Building on Anderson’s concept of imagined communities and Ball-Rokeach’s work on Communication Infrastructure Theory, we demonstrate how cartographic mapping can be used to help communities understand how the media construct their geographic area. We compare media coverage to other datasets about particular geographies, documenting gaps between the two. We do this work through four case studies. Each case study illustrates a unique way in which external data can be compared to coverage. We compare media coverage of Philadelphia locations to how many people live in various regions, the issues emphasized in the media and those that Philadelphia residents say are important for their neighborhoods, media coverage of crime that mentions various locations to crime statistics in Chicago, and data about the number of COVID cases in different parts of Chicago to news organizations’ Facebook posts about the disease. The gaps revealed by these analyses, we propose, allow for reflection on whether media coverage is serving the needs of communities. We conclude by discussing lessons learned about using mapping across these projects, and how similar studies can be used by communities and newsrooms.

item.title: (In)congruent synergies? Discursive boundary-spanning between the Italian anti-gender galaxy and anti-trans groups
item.dc:creator: Elena Pavan, Aurora Perego, Matteo Scianna
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Elena Pavan, Aurora Perego, Matteo Scianna

Topics: Social media, Political polarization, Gender representation, Media framing

This article investigates increasing alignment between the anti-gender galaxy and anti-trans groups by looking at the symbolic synergies that these two collective endeavors create in and through social media discourse. Building on social movement theory, we examine processes of discursive boundary spanning through which ecclesial and right-wing actors, dedicated anti-gender organizations, and anti-trans groups converge when discussing gender-related issues at large on social media, aligning around similar agendas, objects of interest, priorities, and frames, while setting aside differences that might hinder their collaboration. Empirically, the study relies on a mixed-method analysis of Facebook and Instagram posts published between 2021 and 2023 by twenty-two prominent actors mobilizing around anti-gender and anti-trans claims in Italy. Combining topic modeling with a computational adaptation of frame semantic grammar and qualitative frame analysis, we examine patterns of discursive convergence across the four sectors as well as the ideological differences that are bracketed to sustain it. Our findings reveal the existence of a transversal and yet fragile cross-sectoral discursive convergence. While all four sectors align around a limited set of shared interests and priorities, stronger discursive commonalities are found between anti-trans actors, dedicated anti-gender organizations and right-wing actors. Moreover, although common diagnostic frames emphasize the protection of women and children from gender ideology, divergent prognostic frames and long-term horizons persist within and across sectors.

item.title: Who Verifies the Verifiers? AI, Local Knowledge Production, and Credibility in Tanzania’s 2025 Election
item.dc:creator: Gregory Gondwe
item.description:
Political Communication · Gregory Gondwe

Topics: Fact-checking, Misinformation, Artificial intelligence, Political communication

This study examines how Factchecking AI tools and community-based credibility practices interacted during Tanzania’s 2025 presidential election. Using data from five regions, we analyzed 342 media materials, 87 interviews, field observations, and 22 distinct contested election events. The findings identify three forms of verification disjuncture. First, AI-assisted translation and transcription sometimes changed the meaning of politically important statements before journalists could verify them. Second, fact-checks and disputed claims often moved through different communication channels, which limited the chances that people would see the correction. Third, some communities trusted personal experience, familiar sources, and collective discussion more than professional fact-checkers. Participants judged credibility through relationships, lived experience, group discussion, humor and satire, and social accountability. These practices sometimes supported the same conclusions as institutional verification and sometimes produced different judgments. We argue that fact-checking becomes politically effective when the meaning of a claim is preserved, the correction reaches the people discussing it, and the source of the correction is recognized as credible. This explains why an accurate fact-check can still have limited public influence.

item.title: Hearts for hating Activists: how far-right actors dominate polarized TikTok debates on climate protest
item.dc:creator: Hendrik Meyer
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Hendrik Meyer

Topics: TikTok, Political polarization, Climate change communication, Social movements

This study investigates degrees of polarization in political climate protest debates on TikTok. Drawing on a dataset of automatically transcribed TikTok videos posted by German politicians between 2022 and 2025 (N ≈ 1,700), alongside associated user comments (N ≈ 53,000), this study compares discussions on general climate activism, reformist activism (Fridays for Future), and disruptive activism (Letzte Generation). Using a mixed-method approach that combines Large Language Model-based frame classification, stance detection, and network analysis, this study operationalizes Discursive Polarization across ideological, affective, and interactional dimensions. Findings reveal that while all protest debates on TikTok are polarized, disruptive protests are associated with particularly intense attacks and less attention to policy-oriented climate discussions. However, conservative and far-right politicians consistently frame all activist groups as extremists, criminals, or threats to public order, with far-right accounts dominating content production and audience support. Network analyses demonstrate that far-right politicians and their supporters form highly connected clusters in which both emotionally positive and hostile user engagement amplifies elite-level antagonism. Even moderate posts by center-left or progressive politicians attract disproportionate backlash, suggesting asymmetric polarization dynamics linked to partisan user networks. Overall, the study shows that political TikTok debates around climate protest are consistently polarized along ideological lines, but that greater disruptiveness coincides with more intense antagonistic engagement and weaker Connective Action among supporters. Most crucially, far-right politicians emerge as the clear beneficiaries of this polarization, occupying central positions in antagonist networks of Connective Counteraction and dominating the debate through disruption.

item.title: Too Much or Not Enough? The Decline of the Iconic News Image and the Adaptive Challenges of Visual Digital Journalism
item.dc:creator: Ellie Macdonald
item.description:
Digital Journalism · Ellie Macdonald

Topics: Visual journalism, Digital media, Generative AI, News coverage

Iconic news images have traditionally played a central role in journalistic praxis and public discourse, transcending news cycles and forming shared visual narratives. However, in contemporary digital media ecologies, single images struggle to gain traction amid multimedia storytelling, divergent editorial priorities, and dynamic platform affordances. To investigate the adaptive context of this shift, this article presents a case study of photographic reporting on the Israel-Palestine conflict from October 2023 to March 2024, analysing lead images from Al Jazeera English, The Guardian, and BBC News. While some unifying themes were evident, the outlets tended not to republish single images, instead favouring a high volume of imagery alongside multimedia content. In contrast, the viral circulation of a related AI-generated image indicates the continued importance of symbolic condensation within contemporary visual discourse. As such, the widespread circulation of this image illustrates how adaptive behaviours within a complex system can incite visual coherence outwith journalistic production. The image therefore signals a potential risk: in the absence of effective journalistic adaptation, the civic function of iconic news photographs could be displaced by epistemically synthetic imagery; loosening the connection between iconic visual symbolism and photographic witnessing.

item.title: From Grassroots Sleuthing to Global Uptake: Epistemic Legitimation of Open-Source Investigations in Journalism Through Mediazona’s War Casualty Project in Russia’s War on Ukraine
item.dc:creator: Volha Kananovich
item.description:
Digital Journalism · Volha Kananovich

Topics: Open-source investigation, Journalism, Epistemic authority, Digital journalism

This study examines how open-source investigation (OSINV) is legitimized within journalism through an analysis of a casualty-counting project by Mediazona, an exiled independent Russian newsroom documenting Russian military deaths in Ukraine. Drawing on Mediazona’s public-facing project materials and coverage by seven international news organizations, the analysis traces how epistemic authority is established and re-anchored as the project circulates across journalistic institutions. The findings show that Mediazona constructs epistemic authority through a rich epistemic repertoire grounded in procedural rigor, radical transparency, and aesthetic sense-making. As the project gains global uptake, however, these articulations do not circulate intact. Instead, news organizations selectively mobilize elements of Mediazona’s epistemic repertoire in ways that reflect their editorial routines, epistemological commitments, audience expectations, and culturally resonant interpretive frames. In this process, Mediazona’s epistemic labor—and that of its citizen contributors, whom news organizations consistently avoid labeling “sleuths”—receives varying degrees of recognition: elevated as that of an independent outlet, absorbed into the institutional authority of international collaborators, or folded into professional routines that recast the project through a data-journalistic vocabulary and original field reporting. Taken together, the findings show that OSINV legitimation is uneven and context-dependent, shifting away from amateurist connotations toward more methodologically disciplined epistemic labor.

item.title: The Relational Costs of Asymmetric Mixed Reality Headset Use in Large Groups
item.dc:creator: Monique Santoso, Portia Wang, Jeremy N. Bailenson
item.description:
Media Psychology · Monique Santoso, Portia Wang, Jeremy N. Bailenson

Topics: Mixed reality, Virtual reality, Interpersonal communication, Social presence

Mixed reality (MR) technologies are increasingly used in classrooms, workplaces, and collaborative environments, yet little is known about how asymmetric headset use, that is, when some interactants wear headsets and others do not within the same group, shapes interpersonal perception. Guided by uncertainty reduction theory (URT), this study examined how headset use and familiarity jointly influence social presence, closeness, ostracism, and group interaction dynamics in face-to-face MR group collaboration. University students (N = 101) were assigned to groups of 9–10 participants to either wear a headset or not before engaging in a discussion task. Compared to participants with headsets, participants without headsets felt less close to and less present with headset-wearing partners. In contrast, headset wearers, who could see the other group members via passthrough video, did not exhibit parallel decreases. Behavioral analyses showed a crossover pattern in compromise behavior, where individuals who wore a headset compromised more in unfamiliar settings (i.e. where they rated group members less familiar) but those who did not wear a headset compromised more in familiar settings, suggesting that individuals adapt communication strategies to manage uncertainty in asymmetric MR environments. Overall, MR headsets selectively affected interpersonal connection and group dynamics.

item.title: Data benefits? Attitudes and aspirations of recipients towards social security administrative data sharing
item.dc:creator: Victoria Gorton, Morgan E. Currie
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Victoria Gorton, Morgan E. Currie

Topics: Public attitudes, Trust, Digital inequality, Data sharing

This paper outlines benefit recipients’ views towards the sharing of data that is collected about them when they routinely interact with social security services. Sharing this administrative data between public bodies promises to transform the delivery and evaluation of social security. However, there remains a lack of research into public attitudes, understandings, and aspirations for the sharing of this data, particularly from those whose data would be shared. Drawing on discussions from deliberative focus groups with 41 individuals, we reflect on the scope for increased data sharing to deliver improvements for recipients.While participants were aware of how their data is currently shared and how increased data sharing might have advantages, they expressed strong distrust in government agencies to manage their data and concerns about being placed in a position of increased vulnerability. We argue individuals’ views towards data sharing cannot be separated from their lived experiences of data systems – their data realities – which are often markedly different from system designers. We conclude by offering considerations against data systems re-introducing paternalistic policy, unintentionally, via automation – which we term ‘automated paternalism’.

item.title: From mobilization to diversion: a comparative study of wartime communication tactics of Ukrainian and Russian political elites on Telegram
item.dc:creator: Mykola Makhortykh, Aytalina Kulichkina, Kateryna Maikovska
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Mykola Makhortykh, Aytalina Kulichkina, Kateryna Maikovska

Topics: Political communication, Telegram, Crisis communication, Political polarization

This study examines how Ukrainian and Russian political elites communicate on Telegram during the ongoing Russo-Ukrainian war. Using a dataset of Telegram public posts from 2019 to 2024, we analyze changes in communication volume, thematic content, and actor engagement before and after Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion. While the invasion triggered a massive spike in elites’ activity on Telegram in both countries—most notably among actors associated with Russia’s ruling pro-regime party—the focus of this communication diverged sharply. While Ukrainian elites initially prioritized war-related mobilization, this emphasis has declined over time. By contrast, Russian elites from the start adopted a tactic of strategic diversion, avoiding discussion of the war and shifting public attention to unrelated issues, such as crises in the West. Finally, we show that communication patterns are stratified by party size, with smaller parties specializing in narrow policy niches. These findings shed light on how political elites adapt their communication strategies in online environments during wartime.

item.title: Trust in algorithms biased appraisal and boosted affect in online dating
item.dc:creator: Jian Ming Hu, Yoo Jung Oh
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Jian Ming Hu, Yoo Jung Oh

Topics: Online dating, Trust, Algorithmic curation, Social media algorithms

The algorithmification of social encounters is a topic of immense scholarly interest. People often form layperson beliefs about how algorithms work, which can predict how people psychologically navigate algorithmic social encounters. Online dating scholars have drawn upon correlational findings to speculate that trust in algorithms primes daters to think and feel about their dating experiences in certain ways. Within a sample of U.S. adults (N = 165), we experimentally test this speculation by manipulating participants’ trusting beliefs in the efficacy of algorithms (high vs. low), assigning them to evaluate online dating profiles drawn from the same pool, and observing whether appraisal and emotion differed between conditions. Post profile evaluation, high-belief participants perceived higher online dating success than low-belief participants. In turn, more successful participants felt more self-assured and jovial, and meanwhile less anxious or sad. Our study is the first to experimentally examine trusting beliefs in dating algorithms. Findings suggest a self-fulfilling prophecy of beliefs about algorithmic social processes and warrant more future investigation.

item.title: Between Journalism and Justice: Disciplinary Humility in Open-Source Investigations
item.dc:creator: Isabella Regan, Imar de Vries
item.description:
Digital Journalism · Isabella Regan, Imar de Vries

Topics: Journalism, Open-source investigations, Professional norms, Digital journalism

Open-source investigations (OSI) have become an increasingly influential method for reporting on conflict, documenting human rights violations, and supporting justice and accountability efforts. As the field has matured, OSI practitioners have increasingly operated across journalistic, legal, human rights, and technical domains, creating innovation and collaboration opportunities, but also disciplinary tensions. Despite growing scholarship on the institutionalization of OSI, less attention has been paid to how practitioners navigate overlapping disciplinary mandates. Drawing on interviews with 35 practitioners involved in OSI across journalism, human rights, law enforcement and specialized investigative organizations, this article examines how disciplinary boundaries are experienced and responded to within justice and accountability contexts. The findings show that practitioners respond to tensions between journalistic and legal norms through forms of boundary recalibration, including recognizing disciplinary limitations and restructuring investigative work. To explain these dynamics, this article introduces disciplinary humility, defined as the recognition of the limits of one’s disciplinary expertise and mandate when operating across overlapping professional jurisdictions. The article contributes to digital journalism scholarship by showing that the OSI institutionalization is shaped not only by hybridity and boundary crossing, but also by boundary recalibration through which practitioners re-examine expertise and mandates across journalistic and legal contexts.

item.title: Between Ideals and BoPo: Daily Associations Between Exposure to Appearance Content and Body Image Among Young Individuals with Visible Differences
item.dc:creator: Laure Dedecker, L. Coosemans, Chelly Maes, Lara Schreurs, Laura Vandenbosch
item.description:
Media Psychology · Laure Dedecker, L. Coosemans, Chelly Maes, Lara Schreurs, Laura Vandenbosch

Topics: Body image, Social media use, Social media algorithms, Mental health

Exposure to appearance-related content, including beauty ideals and body positivity (BoPo) elements, is linked to young individuals’ body image. Despite being challenged to develop a healthy body image, research has overlooked young individuals with visible differences. This daily diary study among a community-recruited sample of 117 Dutch-speaking (i.e. 110 Belgians, 7 Dutch) young individuals with visible differences (Mage = 25.41), therefore, examined the short-term relationships between exposure to beauty ideals and BoPo elements with/without visible differences and appearance satisfaction, and body/visible difference surveillance. Also, the moderating role of protective filtering was explored. Multilevel regression models showed that on days when participants saw more beauty ideals without visible differences, they showed less appearance satisfaction, and higher body/visible difference surveillance, compared to their typical daily exposure and body image levels. Protective filtering moderated this association: individuals high in protective filtering experienced smaller decreases in appearance satisfaction. No between- or other within-person associations emerged. These findings highlight the complexity of social media exposure for the body image of young individuals with visible differences and the value of enhancing their protective filtering.

item.title: The Politics of the “Non-Political”: A Conceptual Review
item.dc:creator: Yufan Guo, Yibin Fan
item.description:
Political Communication · Yufan Guo, Yibin Fan

Topics: Political communication, Communication theory, Political polarization, Depoliticization

Recent literature has documented a growing entanglement between political processes and many nonpolitical entities. This calls into question the traditional presupposition of politics as a self-contained sphere, highlighting the need to clarify how the conceptual relationship between the political and the nonpolitical has been established. In line with a relational understanding of politics, we provide a boundary analysis by looking at the “non-political” labeling in 140 empirical studies published in political science and communication journals. Two major conceptual treatments are identified: categorical, treating the “non-political” as an inherent, exclusive feature; and contextual, viewing it as a temporary, transformative state. Intellectual traditions, theoretical orientations, methodological standards, and rhetorical norms in academic knowledge production may explain why this boundary has been constructed in such different ways. We call for a more active reconciliation between these treatments, and argue that the nonpolitical, as well as (de)politicization, should be recognized as a meaningful analytical lens. It signifies a relational stance against the explicit, institutionalized politics in political communication studies, offering an indirect yet heuristically productive response to the question of what the political is.

item.title: “Hogwarts is My Home.” The Influence of Transportation, Identification, and Emotion-Specific Personality Traits on the Perceived Sense of Heimat in Fictional Media Worlds
item.dc:creator: Holger Schramm, Julia Grunwald
item.description:
Journal of Broadcasting & Electronic Media · Holger Schramm, Julia Grunwald

Topics: Parasocial relationships, Media psychology, Uses and gratifications, Well-being

In the course of globalization, people are often uprooted from their geographical homes and satisfy their need for a sense of home (sense of Heimat) through alternative sources. Until now, fictional media worlds have hardly been studied in this context, even though fiction has been shown to satisfy social needs. The results of a stimulus-based online survey, in which participants watched an excerpt from the film “Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone,” show that transportation into the fictional world and identification with Harry Potter can promote a sense of Heimat and, as a result, positive affect.

item.title: Young people and the data gaze: experiencing datafication in everyday life
item.dc:creator: Julia E. Coffey, Steven Threadgold
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Julia E. Coffey, Steven Threadgold

Topics: Datafication, Digital media, Young people, Digital platforms

Young people’s capacity to see and know themselves is increasingly informed by algorithmic and classificatory logics. In this article, we extend Beer’s concept of the data gaze, drawing from qualitative empirical examples to illustrate how young people navigate and incorporate datafied ways of seeing and knowing in their everyday practices via engagement with financial technology (fintech) and photo editing apps. We argue that whilst young people are increasingly ‘gazed upon’ in their interactions with fintech and image-editing apps, that is, categorised and imagined by algorithmic and machinic processes, they also gaze back. We explore two specific aspects of the broader data gaze: (1) datafied money and the financialised gaze that young people experience when being nudged while using gamified fintech services, and (2) datafied bodies and the forensic gaze young people use to inform selfie-editing practices through digital ‘corrections’ to their faces and bodies. The implications of these ever-finer capacities for predictive classificatory processes are essential for understanding how life feels under the gaze of the data industry, and how inequalities and exclusions are made, automated and remade in contemporary datafied lives.

item.title: Does Immersive Journalism Erode News Objectivity? Effects of Immersion on Audience Emotional Engagement and Objectivity Perception
item.dc:creator: Qi Zhou, Zongya Li
item.description:
Digital Journalism · Qi Zhou, Zongya Li

Topics: Journalism, Journalistic practice, Digital journalism, Media effects

Immersive journalism’s potential to foster empathy and engagement has been widely highlighted. However, its impact on the core journalistic norm of objectivity remains critically underexplored. Drawing on a value perception framework, this study examines how immersive news affects enjoyment, alertness, and perceived active objectivity in risk communication. Two between-subjects experiments compared MR-enhanced news with 2D news and high- with low-immersion MR news. Results show that immersion consistently increased enjoyment but reduced alertness. However, the studies did not provide consistent evidence that immersion directly enhances or erodes perceived active objectivity. Instead, more robust pattern emerged through indirect pathways: enjoyment was negatively associated with perceived active objectivity, whereas alertness was positively associated with it. Exploratory moderation analysis further suggests that spatial distance may shape these affective pathways. This study advances a novel value perception framework to digital journalism and demonstrates the interplay effect of immersive strategies and audience characteristics in journalism persuasion.

item.title: Moral Archivists and Agents of Accountability: Typologies of Advocacy Journalism in Local Indonesian Media's Coverage of the Kanjuruhan Tragedy
item.dc:creator: Reza Safitri, Dicky Wahyudi, Ainun Qisthi Rosyidah, Ranee Tuta
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Reza Safitri, Dicky Wahyudi, Ainun Qisthi Rosyidah, Ranee Tuta

Topics: Advocacy journalism, Local media, Journalistic practice, Journalistic roles

This study examines how local media implemented advocacy journalism in their coverage of the Kanjuruhan Tragedy, an event that killed 135 people and triggered prolonged collective trauma in Malang, Indonesia. Using a qualitative approach, the study analyzed 160 news articles and conducted in-depth interviews with journalists and editors from four local media outlets. The findings identify six typologies of advocacy journalism that are not isolated but interconnected, forming a dynamic spectrum of practices. Segmented Advocacy emerges as the dominant form through the direct representation of victims’ voices, often integrated with Emotional Advocacy to build public empathy. Meanwhile, Woven Advocacy and Counter-Frame Advocacy demonstrate strategic critiques that range from implicit to explicit challenges to state narratives. Emerging new typologies and Community Alliance further indicate the expansion of advocacy into cultural, spiritual, and collaborative engagement with civil society. The findings also reveal that institutional pressures and journalist polarization dynamics shape advocacy practices. These findings offer an empirically grounded perspective on advocacy journalism in the Global South, where local media act as moral archivists and agents of accountability sustaining collective memory and justice.

item.title: Does the TikTok Feed Lean Right? Exposure to Political Content Among Non-Partisan Users in Germany
item.dc:creator: Jasper Tjaden, Johannes Wolfgram, Aaron Philipp, Sarah Weissmann, Licia Bobzien, Ulrich Köhler, Roland Verwiebe
item.description:
Political Communication · Jasper Tjaden, Johannes Wolfgram, Aaron Philipp, Sarah Weissmann, Licia Bobzien, Ulrich Köhler, Roland Verwiebe

Topics: TikTok, Political content exposure, Algorithmic curation, Political polarization

Populist parties are gaining popularity among young voters in many Western democracies. Young voters increasingly obtain news online through social media websites. TikTok has quickly ascended to become one of the most popular platforms globally. We evaluate exposure disparities regarding political parties by measuring the extent to which parties enter non-partisan users’ feeds. By implementing a sock puppet audit using 78 automated users, we can hold individual user behaviour constant – the main mechanisms through which platform algorithms curate user feeds. We collect data in Germany ahead of the three regional elections in 2024 and the federal election in 2025 (N= 561.000 videos). Overall, political content constitutes 4-10% of user feeds in our sample. When non-partisan users encounter (unsolicited) political content, it is more likely to feature videos posted by or supportive of the far-right, populist Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party than moderate parties. Further evidence on mechanisms explaining this right-wing visibility advantage points to the importance of multiplier networks and content virality.

item.title: “They Don’t Understand What it Means to be Poor”: How Representation, Relevance, and Relatability Shape the News Experience of Marginalised Young Adults
item.dc:creator: James Dennis
item.description:
Journalism Studies · James Dennis

Topics: News avoidance, Journalism, Social media, Media representation

There are significant concerns about young adults from low socioeconomic backgrounds becoming disengaged from the news. Drawing on 25 semi-structured interviews with participants aged 18–25 in England, this study examines how social inequality shapes how young adults experience news. Interviewees avoid legacy news media, citing a lack of representation, as stories about them and their communities are omitted from coverage. Where relevant topics are included, they feel that the reporting masks the complexity of how an issue impacts marginalised communities. Crucially, however, this group are not consistent news avoiders but remains engaged with news found on social platforms, accessing perspectives that resonate with their lived experience. This often comes from non-traditional actors who draw on new forms of journalistic storytelling. This paper argues that relatability—understood as a felt sense of proximity to news based on shared communicative norms, cultural experiences, and perceived social relevance—is crucial to understanding this population's news experience. By analysing relatability alongside representation and relevance, the study demonstrates how the interviewees’ lived experience of inequality shapes their relationship to news, both in its content and form. The paper offers practical recommendations for how inclusive storytelling and support for creator journalists can better serve this population.

item.title: Claiming sociodigital futures? Knowledge practices and their consequences
item.dc:creator: Susan Halford, Kirsten F. Cater, Sabine Hauert, Rasheed Hussain, Daniel McQuillan, Weiru Liu
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Susan Halford, Kirsten F. Cater, Sabine Hauert, Rasheed Hussain, Daniel McQuillan, Weiru Liu

Topics: Sociotechnical imaginaries, Digital media, Knowledge practices, Sociology of expectations

There is currently intense and widespread speculation about the implications of digital technologies for future societies, despite a wealth of evidence that past claims to predict how technology will shape the future have usually failed. Nonetheless, it is now well established that claims to knowledge about how emerging technologies will shape future worlds are performative, exercising powerful effects on the futures they claim to describe. Building on the Sociology of Expectations and work on Sociotechnical Imaginaries, this paper turns attention to the ontological and epistemological ‘nuts’ and ‘bolts’ of claims about digital technologies, social life and the future. We ask: how are these entities and the relations between them constituted and given traction as knowledge practices? Specifically, we explore the practices used by major future-claiming institutional actors in a selection of published documents. We find a strikingly coherent ontological performance of the relations between ‘the digital’, ‘the social’ and ‘the future’ and the circulation of (what comes to count as) knowledge across these institutions. Indeed, what is striking is the re-purposability of these knowledge practices despite the distinctive institutional interests in play. These knowledge practices offer a limited grasp on the futures that are currently in the making. Moreover, they enable the persistence of a latent set of assumptions which are powerful in limiting consideration of critical questions about the future.

item.title: From Facebook to front page: the influence of the Gilets Jaunes’ social media on local press language and framing
item.dc:creator: Davide Morselli, Maite Beramendi, Olivier Fillieule
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Davide Morselli, Maite Beramendi, Olivier Fillieule

Topics: Social media activism, Media framing, Journalism, Social movements

This article examines how social media discussions within a protest movement intersect with local news coverage, focusing on the French Gilets Jaunes in the Var department. We hypothesize that journalistic language may progressively align with activists’ semantic universe, thereby contributing to the diffusion of movement claims and terminology. We analyze activists’ Facebook discussions and reporting by the regional daily Var-Matin between 2018 and 2021. Study 1 combines qualitative analysis of reciprocal mentions between Facebook groups and press articles to document mechanisms of interdependence. It shows that local journalists routinely relied on Facebook as a source of information about the movement’s activities and claims, using activists’ online discussions both to anticipate protest events and to contextualize them. Study 2 applies word embeddings to measure semantic proximity between activist and journalistic discourse over time. Results reveal a selective and time-structured semantic convergence consistent with journalists’ sustained exposure to activists’ internal communication. Although Facebook discussions gradually shifted away from some initial claims, local press coverage repeatedly mobilized these founding frames whenever the movement re-entered the news agenda. At the local level, these findings refine the protest paradigm by showing that coverage emphasized protesters’ motivations.

item.title: Whose voices and which effects? A scoping review of migration and social media effects
item.dc:creator: Aleksandra Lazić, Maryam Khaleghipour, Jörg Matthes
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Aleksandra Lazić, Maryam Khaleghipour, Jörg Matthes

Topics: Media effects, Social media, Migration, Differential susceptibility to media effects

Social media plays a central role in shaping migration experiences and public perceptions of migration. However, despite growing research activity, no systematic overview exists on how social media effects are examined across host and migrant populations. This scoping review synthesizes 65 empirical studies on social media effects in the context of migration published between 2020 and 2025. Guided by the differential susceptibility to media effects model, the analysis focuses on content types, sample characteristics, the conceptualization of social media, effect types, and mediating and moderating factors. The findings reveal two largely disconnected strands of research: quantitative, host-focused studies that emphasize negative attitudinal effects, and qualitative, migrant-centered studies that focus on empowerment. Framing effects, platform affordances, producer perspectives, and individual, structural, and social factors remain largely neglected. Overall, the review highlights the need for integrative research that bridges the perspectives of both hosts and migrants and pays greater attention to how migrants themselves perceive, interpret, and respond to social media portrayals and migration-related content.

item.title: Communication strategies and barriers in friends’ mental health conversations on college campuses
item.dc:creator: Aurora Occa, Kelly G. McAninch, Diane B. Francis, Anita Silwal, Hayley M Stahl, Anne Amegbeha Amissah
item.description:
Communication Monographs · Aurora Occa, Kelly G. McAninch, Diane B. Francis, Anita Silwal, Hayley M Stahl, Anne Amegbeha Amissah

Topics: Mental health, College students, Interpersonal communication, Social support

Mental health challenges among college students are common yet difficult to identify and address. Friends often serve as the first line of support, making mental health conversations a critical but understudied intervention avenue. Research has emphasized disclosure over how friends offer support, engage with struggling peers, or handle emotional and relational complexities. These interactions is less studied. We conducted 10 focus groups (N = 68) to examine strategies friends use to navigate mental health conversations and identify facilitating and hindering factors. Participants identified signs of distress, created safe spaces, used direct and indirect strategies to foster conversation, attended to timing, and prioritized protection. Individual, relational, contextual, and societal factors shaped these conversations. We discuss conceptual and practical implications and propose future research.

item.title: Perceiving the News as Toxic: A Longitudinal, Cross-National Analysis of Negative News Evaluations in Flanders and Ireland
item.dc:creator: Pauljan Truyens, Cassandra Craig, Eirini Evangelia Psychari, Ike Picone, John O’Sullivan, Paul McNamara
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Pauljan Truyens, Cassandra Craig, Eirini Evangelia Psychari, Ike Picone, John O’Sullivan, Paul McNamara

Topics: News avoidance, News consumption, Fake news, Longitudinal study

In today’s media environment, where information overload, negativity, and news fatigue are increasingly common, news can feel toxic. Yet little research examines how users perceive this toxicity and adjust their news practices in response. This study addresses that gap through a repeated cross-sectional analysis of Flanders and Ireland. Drawing on DNR-data from 2017-2025 and latent class analysis, we identify three archetypal news repertoires: Panoramic, Limited, and Traditional. Our findings reveal a shift toward limited repertoires, particularly among younger and less socioeconomically advantaged groups, while panoramic repertoires have become rarer, and traditional repertoires have remained stable. These shifts are associated with negative news attitudes, including distrust, avoidance, disinterest, fake news concerns and perceived fake news exposure. The cross-national comparison highlights sharper transitions in Flanders, whereas Irish users retained higher engagement, though early disengagement emerged. By linking negative attitudes or evaluations with changes in repertoires, we contribute to audience research and underscore the need to reconsider the journalism-audience relationship as disengagement is no longer marginal but increasingly mainstream. From a user perspective, repertoire narrowing may be understood as a coping response, although it risks deepening informational inequalities.

item.title: When Populism? Consistent and Opportunistic Populist Communication in the 2022 Brazilian Presidential Elections
item.dc:creator: Gustavo Luiz Venturelli, Paolo Ricci, Guilherme Tiengo, Raphaela Velho
item.description:
Political Communication · Gustavo Luiz Venturelli, Paolo Ricci, Guilherme Tiengo, Raphaela Velho

Topics: Populism, Political communication, Election campaigns, Computational methods

When do presidential candidates use populist communication, and does its prevalence vary across policy domains? We address these questions using an original dataset of 11,885 tweets from nine Brazilian presidential candidates during the 2022 elections. Drawing on the ideational approach, we operationalize populist discourse as the co-occurrence of people-centrism and anti-elitism, measured with fine-tuned BERT-based classifiers, and classify policy domains with the Comparative Agendas Project framework. Our findings reveal substantial heterogeneity across candidates, challenging expectations that populist communication uniformly intensifies during campaigns or systematically varies across policy domains according to ideology. Rather than increasing uniformly during the campaign, populist appeals escalate strategically for some candidates as elections approach, while remaining stable for others throughout the electoral year. We propose a typology distinguishing opportunistic from consistent populists. Across policy domains, government operations serve as a baseline facilitating populist framing. Left-wing candidates increase populist rhetoric in labor/employment, consistent with issue ownership expectations, but right-wing candidates reduce populist appeals in their traditionally owned domains of law and crime and civil rights, contrary to expectations. Overall, we show that populism is neither a universal campaign imperative nor a content-neutral communication style, but a flexible discursive frame shaped by candidate strategy, electoral context, and policy content.

item.title: Skewed toward uniformity? Investigating algorithmic stereotyping and amplification in AI-generated images
item.dc:creator: Daniela Mahl, Lars Guenther
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Daniela Mahl, Lars Guenther

Topics: Artificial intelligence, Generative AI, Media representation, Algorithmic curation

As text-to-image generative artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes visual communication, concerns are growing about its role in reproducing social stereotypes. While recent algorithm auditing studies have advanced our understanding of stereotypical AI-generated imagery, they have largely focused on a narrow set of stereotypes – primarily gender and race – overlooking more nuanced forms. Addressing this gap, our study adopts a case-sensitive approach that conceptualizes stereotypes as multi-layered phenomena composed of multiple, context-specific indicators. Applying the Draw-a-Scientist Test framework, we analyzed stereotypical representations of scientists in images generated by DALL·E 3 and examined potential amplification by benchmarking against Google Images. Specifically, we compared 16 stereotype indicators across six stereotype subjects. Using Latent Class Analysis, we identified six classes reflecting distinct patterns of stereotypical depiction. Our findings show that DALL·E not only produces highly stereotypical portrayals of scientists but also amplifies these patterns compared to Google Images. Both image sources lack adequate visual references for disciplines beyond the traditional laboratory context – a pattern we interpret as epistemic narrowing, whereby diverse forms of knowledge production are reduced to a uniform, laboratory-based representation of science. We conclude by discussing potential drivers of epistemic narrowing, the broader implications of algorithmic visibility, and mitigation strategies.

item.title: From constituencies to audiences: lessons from Brazil about audience analytics in representative politics
item.dc:creator: André K. Rodarte
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · André K. Rodarte

Topics: Political communication, Audience perception, Mediatization, Social media use

The pursuit of audiences is a key driver of the mediatization of politics, yet it remains unclear how parliamentarians carry out this task. Drawing on interviews with members of Brazil’s Congress, this study investigates how politicians incorporate audience analytics into their communication strategies. It introduces a conceptual framework of audience perception – distinguishing among loyalists, followers, and audience reservoirs – to explain how politicians interpret digital publics. Findings reveal that parliamentarians’ perceptions of their audiences differ from their perceptions of electoral bases. Their follower base undergoes context collapse, disembedding audiences from their social context. Digital media re-embed these constituencies in platform contexts, wherein parliamentarians believe they must become always-on content producers, perform authenticity, and engage in information cycles. These findings reveal that audience analytics incentivize a sales orientation in parliamentary communication, distorting representation by recasting audiences as targets of influence rather than publics to whom politicians are accountable.

item.title: Immersion Matters: Virtual Reality Influences Personal and Systemic Bias Outcomes
item.dc:creator: Elisabeth S. Noland, Christopher R. Agnew, Margo J. Monteith
item.description:
Media Psychology · Elisabeth S. Noland, Christopher R. Agnew, Margo J. Monteith

Topics: Virtual reality, Racial bias, Empathy, Media effects

Social psychological research has used traditional empathy-inducing strategies (e.g. reading, listening to, or watching narratives) to heighten recognition of and motivation to combat personal and systemic bias. We investigated whether a non-embodied 360° virtual reality (VR) experience increased recognition of and motivation to combat both personal and systemic racial bias and examined empathy as an underlying mechanism. Non-Black undergraduates in the United States (N = 313) were randomly assigned to (a) a non-embodied immersive 360° VR experience depicting racial discrimination, (b) an audio-only version of the same experience, or (c) a race-unrelated audio (control). VR exposure (vs. audio-only and control) heightened recognition of systemic bias, motivation to combat both systemic and personal bias, and perceptions of racism in isolated incidents. Emotional empathy, but not cognitive empathy, was a significant mediator. In contrast, the audio-only condition did not differ from the VR or control condition on personal and systemic bias outcomes or recognition of racism. These findings highlight the theoretical and practical value of non-embodied 360° immersive VR as a tool for combating personal and systemic bias.

item.title: Algorithmic News Selection Under News Avoidance: Assessing News Values on Chinese Tiktok (Douyin)
item.dc:creator: Jinhui Li, Wen Shi
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Jinhui Li, Wen Shi

Topics: News avoidance, Algorithmic curation, Social media algorithms, News values

This study explores how recommendation algorithms on Douyin respond to users’ growing disengagement from news by shaping the visibility of news content.
