Adopting an agent-based testing (ABT) approach, we conducted a 2 (intentional news avoidance: 0% vs. 100%) × 2 (unintentional news avoidance: 50% vs. 100%) between-subject experiment to simulate distinct user behaviors and capture large-scale data from news-related videos. Findings indicated that two avoidance behavioral patterns result in contrasting algorithmic outcomes which reinforce or weaken certain news values such as prominence, uniqueness, timeliness, and influence. A significant interaction effect further reveals that the influence of intentional news avoidance on the news values of influence diminishes as users’ preference for non-news content increases, whereas its influence on uniqueness becomes stronger. These findings show that recommender systems adapt to user disengagement by reprioritizing content, highlighting algorithmic curation as a socio-technical process that shapes attention amid selective news exposure.

item.title: Soft Power from the Outside, Career Choice from the Inside: Understanding Job Attractions of Chinese Media Expats in Thailand
item.dc:creator: Tucker Wang-Hai
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Tucker Wang-Hai

Topics: Journalism, Professional identity, Media systems, Journalistic practice

China’s global media expansion is often interpreted as a state-led soft power strategy. Yet little is known about how individual journalists enact this expansion while working overseas for Chinese media organizations. Taking Thailand as an empirical case, this article examines how Chinese journalists assigned to overseas postings come to view their roles as a worthwhile career decision. Drawing on fieldwork conducted in Thailand and in-depth interviews with Chinese expat journalists, it argues that alignment with state goals emerges not from ideological commitment, but from personal motivations, career timing, and everyday practical reasoning. The article draws on Bourdieu’s concept of illusio to conceptualize this process as a socially grounded belief that the pursuit is worth investment. Journalists accept overseas postings insofar as these roles make sense within their own trajectories, at once professionally viable and personally meaningful. The findings complement state-centric models of media expansion and offers a framework for understanding journalists’ on-the-ground motivations amid broader transformations in global journalism.

item.title: The Many Notions of Audience Engagement: A Scoping Review
item.dc:creator: Bernadette Uth
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Bernadette Uth

Topics: Audience engagement, Journalism studies, Engaged journalism, News media

In recent years, “audience engagement” and “engaged journalism” have emerged as buzzwords in journalism studies. Audience engagement is regularly discussed as a potential remedy for declining trust in journalism and its precarious financial situation. Over the past two decades, journalism studies have thus extensively analyzed the concept, resulting in a vast body of literature on engagement. However, this has created definitional confusion around audience engagement, with numerous definitions, interpretations and characteristics of the concept discussed in existing scholarship. By conducting a systematic scoping review of 174 peer-reviewed journal articles on audience engagement, this study sheds closer light on the existing research on engagement, offers an overview on theoretical and empirical conceptualizations, and examines goals and challenges associated with engagement. The review highlights how audience engagement is examined and conceptualized in journalism scholarship, and identifies key directions for future research.

item.title: Black Lives Matter on the Ballot, in the Press: An Argument for Reporting the Long View of Contentious Solutions in Local Journalism
item.dc:creator: Brad Limov, Martin Johannes Riedl, Melissa Santillana, Sharon Strover
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Brad Limov, Martin Johannes Riedl, Melissa Santillana, Sharon Strover

Topics: Journalistic norms, Local journalism, Black Lives Matter, Solutions journalism

This paper investigates how local journalists in Austin, Texas reported on a 2021 ballot initiative mandating increased police staffing. Representing a backlash to 2020 Black Lives Matter protests, the initiative followed efforts to reallocate funds away from the Austin Police Department. Grounded in interviews with journalists who described their news choices and positionality in relation to the initiative, this case study reveals how contentious solutions to intractable social problems exacerbate tensions inherent to dominant journalistic norms. Journalists adhering to impartiality described the initiative’s underlying conflict narrowly to avoid the appearance of bias; more alarmingly, some acted as unfiltered conduits for false information by viewing coverage as a public forum for debate. We evaluate these findings against solutions-oriented journalism—an umbrella term for emerging paradigms that prioritize constructive reporting on solutions to engage news audiences in civic life—and demonstrate how these models fall short when solutions themselves are sites of intense social struggle. Inspired by journalists who resisted norms of impartiality and balance to investigate histories and trajectories of local social action, we encourage proponents of solutions-oriented journalism to prioritize rigorous, factual reporting of the long view for audiences to engage with solutions as people continuously struggle to enact them.

item.title: Journalistic Routines and the Social Construction of Race: A Critical Discourse Analysis of the Tyreek Hill Police Encounter
item.dc:creator: Joseph Jones
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Joseph Jones

Topics: Media framing, Journalistic practice, Discourse analysis, News coverage

To gauge U.S. journalism’s post-2020 racial reckoning, this article examines news coverage of football player Tyreek Hill’s police encounter in September 2024. Using Critical Discourse Analysis to interpret and explain digital media texts, this project mimics the contingency of the internet and considers local, national, legacy, digital-only, and sports outlets. Overall, it finds that news discourse continues to operate through a white racial frame. Even outlets that acknowledged systemic inequities or foregrounded the perspectives of the racially marginalized could recreate this dominant perspective, reinforcing tropes such as Black criminality, victim blaming, and deference to official sources. It’s thus argued that routine journalistic practices such as descriptive reporting, bothsidesism, headline conventions, reliance on official sources, and other supposedly objective norms, actually limit social discourse and the ability to have honest, good faith conversations about race. The project further highlights coverage that did counter the white racial frame and ultimately argues such coverage should be the standard. These practices are more ethical (i.e., take responsibility for the social consequences of news narratives) and provide a more nuanced and rigorous approximation of truth.

item.title: Negotiating Professional Roles in a Constrained Media System: Role Perception and Narrated Enactment among Fact-Checkers in China
item.dc:creator: Hanye Yang
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Hanye Yang

Topics: Journalistic role theory, Fact-checking, Professional norms, Journalistic roles

This study offers the first detailed investigation into how Chinese fact-checkers perceive and narrate the enactment of professional roles within a constrained media environment. Drawing on 14 in-depth, semi-structured interviews with fact-checkers from four types of Chinese fact-checking organizations, the article provides rare qualitative evidence on a professional community that remains difficult to access. The study identifies six roles rooted in the Chinese media context: educator, rumor-buster, curator, independent advocate, gate-watcher, and facilitator. These roles show how fact-checkers negotiate professional ideals, institutional constraints, and national communication priorities in their everyday work. The article contributes to journalistic role theory by linking role perception with narrated role enactment. It shows that professional roles in constrained media systems are not simply adopted or abandoned, but situationally interpreted, negotiated, and combined. Rather than revealing a sharp divide between ideals and practice, the findings suggest a relatively strong convergence between perceived roles and narrated enactment. This convergence reflects the stability of Chinese fact-checkers’ professional self-image under institutional constraint. The article therefore demonstrates how Chinese fact-checkers articulate, justify, and normalize their professional roles, while foregrounding the symbolic and discursive processes through which perception and enactment are connected.

item.title: Taking artificial intelligence from the ‘priesthood’ and providing it as a service: a media-genealogical perspective on big tech’s AI platformisation
item.dc:creator: Inga Luchs
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Inga Luchs

Topics: Platformization, Artificial intelligence, Digital platforms, Media theory

Recently, Amazon, Microsoft, and Google have been positioning artificial intelligence as a utility that should be accessible to everyone. At the same time, they promote their cloud platforms as a means of ‘democratizing’ AI as they distribute easy-to-use AI services at scale. In this article, I propose a media-genealogical approach to situate this claim of ‘democratization’ within a broader development in the infrastructuralisation and platformisation of computing. I focus on three historic moments: (1) the invention of time-sharing and the idea of a ‘computer utility’ in the 1960s; (2) the introduction of abstraction to facilitate software development in the 1970s; and (3) the rise of digital platforms and the provision of user-friendly internet services in the 2000s. I demonstrate how each of these moments of ‘democratization’ is marked by a certain duality: on the one hand, they have expanded access to information technologies through the large-scale distribution of resources and the simplification of complex technologies into services. On the other hand, they have introduced new avenues for the centralisation of power. By means of a critical discourse analysis of Google’s cloud AI platform, I show how cloud companies leverage this duality to forward a process of platformisation, where they establish themselves as the central intermediaries and transform AI technologies into services to be provided at scale. This allows them to increase dependency on their infrastructures and to exert control over technological design. The media-genealogical analysis, finally, points to alternative paths that the democratisation of AI could take.

item.title: Toward a Comprehensive Understanding of Journalists’ Emotional Well-Being: Precarity, Identity and Shared Concern in Latin America
item.dc:creator: Sallie Hughes, Armando Gutiérrez Ortega, Grisel Salazar Rebolledo, Carlos Arcila Calderón, Manasvi Maheshwari, Adriana Amado, Jesús Arroyave, Summer Harlow, Mireya Márquez-Ramírez, Janara Nicoletti
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Sallie Hughes, Armando Gutiérrez Ortega, Grisel Salazar Rebolledo, Carlos Arcila Calderón, Manasvi Maheshwari, Adriana Amado, Jesús Arroyave, Summer Harlow, Mireya Márquez-Ramírez, Janara Nicoletti

Topics: Journalism, Well-being, Precarity, Press freedom

This study examines determinants of journalists’ emotional well-being. Drawing on stress and coping theory, role theory, and research on precarity and safety, it proposes a framework to explain concern about emotional well-being under workplace stress. Data come from the Worlds of Journalism Study in 10 Latin American countries with varying levels of press freedom. The dependent variable is a single-item report of concern about emotional well-being due to work. Hypotheses address gender, precarity, professional roles, victimization, coping, support, and press freedom. Findings show widespread concern driven by structural, organizational, and identity-based vulnerabilities. Indicators of precarity are the strongest predictors: heavier workloads increase concern, while higher income serves as a protective factor. Identity-related factors also matter: identifying as a woman and experiencing workplace bullying—reported more frequently by women—predict higher concern. Role discordance, or tension between self-censorship and professional values, further elevates concern. Unexpectedly, receiving colleague support after attacks is associated with greater concern, suggesting reactive coping or emotional contagion. Press freedom is not a significant predictor. Potential limitations include the single-item outcome and sensitivity of press freedom measures to local conditions. The study calls for organizational interventions while noting that addressing precarity requires structural changes to journalism’s financial model.

item.title: Revisiting the Indian Emergency: Collective Memory and Political Narratives in English-language Dailies
item.dc:creator: Subin Paul
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Subin Paul

Topics: Journalism studies, News coverage, Political communication, Media framing

Although the press is credited with writing the first draft of history, the relevance of the past to journalists as “purveyors of the present” remains less understood, particularly in the Global South. This article grapples with this problem by investigating the uses of the past to journalism. Building on scholarship from journalism and memory studies, I investigate the contemporary news media’s references to the Indian Emergency (1975–1977), in which the government instituted strict controls on freedom of speech and the press. Specifically, by drawing on the concept of “collective memory,” I analyze how mainstream English-language dailies constructed narratives about the Emergency during April-June 2024, a period encompassing the 2024 national election and the anniversary of the Emergency. Narrative analysis reveals two themes in coverage. First, narratives harked back to the Emergency to highlight the ruling government’s suppression of the press in contemporary India. Second, narratives projected the Emergency as a site where political debates and differences between the ruling and opposition parties were played out. This article argues that the narrative use of vernacular linguistic registers, particularly in English-language newswriting, constitutes an important feature of collective memory work and journalistic invocation of the past in this Global South context.

item.title: Does Smartphone Application Use Impact Adolescents’ Affect? Or Vice Versa? An Experience Sampling Study
item.dc:creator: Michaela Šaradín Lebedíková, David Lacko, Michał Tkaczyk, Jana Blahošová, Steriani Elavsky, David Šmahel
item.description:

Topics: Smartphone use, Adolescent mental health, Experience sampling, Well-being

item.title: Digital responsibility, skills and environmental awareness for digital sustainability
item.dc:creator: Maria Laura Ruiu, Massimo Ragnedda, Gabriele Ruiu
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Maria Laura Ruiu, Massimo Ragnedda, Gabriele Ruiu

Topics: Digital literacy, Digital inequality, Digital well-being, Digital media

This study investigates how digital competencies and environmental awareness interact to shape eco-friendly digital practices, contributing to the field of digital sustainability. Drawing on a representative sample of adult internet users in the United Arab Emirates (N = 1016), it explores (H1) whether individual responsibility predicts environmentally conscious digital practices; (H2) whether environmental awareness moderates the effect of perceived digital competence on behavior; and (H3) whether sustainable digital behaviors are associated with perceived digital competence, with awareness as a moderator. Using linear and moderated regression analyses, the findings confirm that individual responsibility is a significant predictor of pro-environmental digital behavior, and that perceived digital competence is positively associated with such behavior, an association that is modestly strengthened, rather than enabled, by environmental awareness. The reverse association, from behavior to perceived digital competence, is not moderated by awareness, pointing to an asymmetrical pattern that the cross-sectional design does not allow us to interpret causally. By integrating digital inequality frameworks with environmental psychology, this study advances the understanding of digital sustainability as a site where perceived competence and responsibility jointly shape sustainable digital engagement.

item.title: Guidance over guidelines? Unpacking the uses and concerns of generative AI in communication science
item.dc:creator: Justin Chun‐ting Ho, Hannes Cools, Joanna Strycharz, A. Marthe Möller, Zeph M. C. van Berlo, Sjoerd B. Stolwijk, Damian Trilling, Theo Araujo
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Justin Chun‐ting Ho, Hannes Cools, Joanna Strycharz, A. Marthe Möller, Zeph M. C. van Berlo, Sjoerd B. Stolwijk, Damian Trilling, Theo Araujo

Topics: Generative AI, Large Language Models, Communication science, Academic publishing

The rapid adoption of generative Artificial Intelligence (genAI) tools has transformed research practices across communication science. As genAI tools (and most notetably large language models), made the generation of text, images, and other media content extremely easy, they can potentially disrupt the way science is conducted. Yet, their integration into academic workflows has outpaced systematic understanding of how, when, and why researchers use them. Drawing on a quantitative survey of N = 1138 communication scientists and four qualitative focus groups, this study provides the first comprehensive mapping of genAI use across communucation research stages and contexts. Findings reveal three key dynamics: a paradox between widespread use and persistent concern; conflicting expectations among individual scholars, institutions, and journals; and the influence of cultural and linguistic contexts on adoption patterns. Together, these findings highlight a multi-level governance challenge encompassing individual, institutional, and disciplinary dimensions. With this paper, we seek to provide a starting point for an open and transparent discussion about the role of generative AI in communication research by proposing a structured set of recommendations for responsible genAI use at three levels: field-wide coordination and collaboration, institutional guidance and support, and individual continuous critical reflection.

item.title: Afterword: the waning power of the fix
item.dc:creator: Noortje Marres
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Noortje Marres

Topics: Digital platforms, Digital transformation, Technology adoption, Digital media

This commentary offers some reflections on the ‘power of the fix' in cybersecurity and its wider implications for technological democracy. I begin with a discussion of the discrepancy between the discourse of solutionism and everyday practices of securing IT systems (Elgaard Jensen et al, 2026). Whereas the former posits that problems are neat and can be solved by means of technology, the latter must confront what Röhle (2021) has called the ‘permanent brokenness' of computational infrastructures. A peculiar form of ‘infrastructural reversal' can then be observed in the field of cybersecurity: here, disruption, breakdown and failure are not the exception, but the default (Collier et al, 2025; Fouad, 2025). This has implications for the role of public disclosure of technological vulnerabilities in the governance of digital systems (Bozzini, 2025). The endemic nature of disruption in computational infrastructures puts at risk the transformative capacities of publicity in technological politics. This also affects social studies of technology insofar as this field has long relied on disruption, failure and breakdown as empirical occasions for making visible how technology works and does not work in practice.

item.title: Political Endorsements by TikTok Influencers: Parasocial Interaction, Identification, and Support for Political Candidates
item.dc:creator: Zicheng Cheng, Homero Gil de Zúñiga
item.description:
Media Psychology · Zicheng Cheng, Homero Gil de Zúñiga

Topics: Political persuasion, Social media influencers, TikTok, Parasocial interaction

This study examines political persuasion on TikTok by testing how influencers’ direct address and media source labels shape audience responses to a political endorsement video. Using a preregistered 2 × 2 online survey experiment with 486 U.S. adults, we found that participants exposed to direct address, defined as the influencer looking directly at the camera, reported significantly higher identification with the influencer and stronger parasocial interaction than those exposed to non-direct address. Drawing on the Entertainment Overcoming Resistance Model, mediation analyses further showed that direct address indirectly increased intention to support the endorsed political candidate through multiple relational and cognitive pathways, including identification, parasocial interaction, counterarguing, perceived norms, and perceived video credibility. By contrast, media source labels did not significantly affect perceived video credibility, did not indirectly influence candidate support, and did not moderate the effects of direct address. These findings point to the importance of relational cues in short-form political influencer communication. By identifying the mechanisms through which influencer content affects attitudes and behavioral intentions, this study advances theory on entertainment-based persuasion and provides practical insights into political communication and influencer politics in short-form media environments.

item.title: Reasserting the Relevance of Media Trust: A Response to Jakobsson and Stiernstedt (2023)
item.dc:creator: Arjen van Dalen
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Arjen van Dalen

Topics: Media trust, Journalism studies, Democratic discourse, News consumption

This article responds to Jakobsson and Stiernstedt's (2023. “Trust and the media: Arguments for the (irr)elevance of a concept.” Journalism Studies 24 (4): 479–495) invitation to critically examine the significance of media trust. They argue that there “is a lack of strong arguments for why falling levels of trust in the news media are legitimately described as a crisis or problem” (479). Their critique offers a valuable counterpoint to the (often implicit) assumption that news media trust is always positive. Still, I argue for closer examination of their central arguments to move toward a comprehensive synthesis. I draw on political science literature and research on the consequences of media trust to reassert the importance of media trust for news consumption, democracy and ontological security. Without a comprehensive synthesis, debate over media trust risks becoming polarized and binary, with scholars selectively citing research that supports their views. The paperproposes two ways forward. First, a dynamic conceptualization of media trust similar to a “thermostat” where media trust provides a baseline openness to information, while vigilance operates as an adaptive regulator, selectively heightening scrutiny. Second, combining cultural and institutional perspectives to develop a more nuanced understanding of the significance of media trust.

item.title: Online activism at odds: Exploring tensions in the everyday practice of ‘professional’ and ‘social media’ activists
item.dc:creator: Victoria Balan, Delia Dumitrica
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Victoria Balan, Delia Dumitrica

Topics: Social media activism, Digital activism, Digital platforms, Social movements

This paper investigates how two groups of activists – ‘professional’ (civil society members) and ‘independent’ activists (using primarily social media for activism) – construct the political power of digital technologies in everyday practice. We focus on how the daily practice of activists draws on both individual experiences and societal macro-discourses to develop a range of discursive resources and subject positions in the symbolic construction of digital activism. Based on a critical discourse analysis of 18 semi-structured interviews, the findings reveal three tensions between discourse and practice, namely: digital activism vs. boots-on-the-ground activism; horizontalism vs. formal organization; and private vs. activist (digital) lives. We argue that despite their persistence, the promises of technology for social justice offered by hegemonic techno-utopian discourses do not neatly fit activist practice. In the complex, messy, and fluid context of everyday life, such promises and ideals are often negotiated, reappropriated, adapted, or rejected by activists. Democratic values are thus not inscribed in technology: local context, organizational structure, and individual factors shape the ways digital technologies help or hinder digital activism. We advise citizen activists to critically consider dominant techno-utopian discourses, particularly their simplified picture of political decision-making processes. Such awareness can better equip citizens when dealing with the tensions generated by their own activist practice.

item.title: Turning a private surveillance service into a public disclosure: the case of Amazon's ring doorbell
item.dc:creator: M.B. Schuilenburg
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · M.B. Schuilenburg

Topics: Surveillance, Privacy, Platform studies, Digital media

This article analyses the interaction between broader political, economic and cultural changes and the local experiences of citizens using the Amazon Ring doorbell. The concept ‘luxury surveillance’ is used to study how citizens engage with the live and recorded images of the Ring doorbell. The paper empirically analyses the impact of the Ring, through (1) observations of platform use, (2) surveys on Facebook, and (3) in-depth interviews (N = 73) with owners of the Ring in four neighbourhoods in Rotterdam, the Netherlands. The findings reveal how the Amazon Ring reframes mundane interactions into mass surveillance opportunities, impacts the presumption of innocence, leads to different forms of perceived privacy, and provides a permanent sense of alertness by the owners.

item.title: Judge, butler, and tool: algorithmic imaginaries and practices of Chinese parent vloggers of autistic children on Douyin
item.dc:creator: Yuchen Ren, Ting Li
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Yuchen Ren, Ting Li

Topics: Algorithmic curation, Social media platforms, Digital media, Mental health

Disability-related new media practices have increasingly attracted scholarly attention. However, existing research often frames user agency in these practices through a binary lens of either ‘empowerment’ or ‘alienation’, insufficiently capturing the complexities of their entanglements with digital technologies. Drawing on the theoretical framework of algorithmic imaginaries, this study investigates how Chinese parent vloggers of autistic children on Douyin imagine and enact their relationships with algorithms. Drawing primarily on in-depth interviews, supplemented by non-participant observation, we found that parent vloggers, driven by both material and spiritual motivations, perceive algorithms as playing three distinct roles: ‘judge,’ ‘butler,’ and ‘tool,’ representing strong, moderate, and weak tensions, respectively. The interplay between these algorithmic imaginaries and parent vloggers’ primary motivations shapes their exercise of agency on Douyin within their new media practices. This study thus calls for reconstructing localized and situated understandings of human–technology relations within disability-related media practices.

item.title: Political Actors and Their Media Practices: Analyzing the Role of Media Participation in Democratic Backsliding and Resilience
item.dc:creator: Daniel Kreiss, Kate Wright
item.description:
Political Communication · Daniel Kreiss, Kate Wright

Topics: Political communication, Media use, Political participation, Disinformation

This paper draws together insights from political science and political communication to advance a new understanding of the role of media in democratic backsliding and resilience. The central argument is that all political actors may also be media actors, although they may do so anonymously or use false identities. Thus, mass participation in media enables mass participation in political change, with better and worse democratic outcomes. As such, when analyzing backsliding and resilience scholars need to move away from focusing solely on particular institutions and actors with presumed democratic functions, as well as assuming that media and expressive freedom will necessarily serve democratic ends. Instead, we advocate analyzing how the participatory media practices of various actors interact with one another via communicative structures within processes of backsliding and resilience. Participatory media practices that prevent democratic breakdown include disseminating early warnings of backsliding, exposing executive errors and corruption, coordinating pro-democratic mobilization, and platforming the opposition, as well as countering disinformation and delegitimizing democratic institutions and processes. We also indicate how participatory media practices may aid democratic bounceback, as well as the challenges involved in reimagining the media infrastructure needed to sustain democratic recovery in the long-term. Thus, we argue that democratic backsliding and resilience should be reconceptualized as profoundly participatory, mediated processes.

item.title: Where belief is filtered: how truthfulness and source credibility shape trust, skepticism, and worry in vaccine communication
item.dc:creator: Viltė Auruškevičienė, Vikas Arya, Ricardo Alexandre Fontes Correia, Dominyka Venciūtė, Vaida Ganytė Oginskytė
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Viltė Auruškevičienė, Vikas Arya, Ricardo Alexandre Fontes Correia, Dominyka Venciūtė, Vaida Ganytė Oginskytė

Topics: Misinformation, Trust, Source credibility, Health communication

This study examines how true versus false messages shape trust in cancer-vaccine information on social media, alongside skepticism and worry, and tests the moderating roles of source credibility and deception-detection self-efficacy. In a 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment (N = 210), participants viewed a simulated cancer-vaccine post and reported their responses. The findings show that true messages elicit significantly higher levels of trust and lower levels of skepticism and worry than false messages, and that source credibility amplifies the positive effect of truthfulness on trust. Source credibility did not, however, moderate skepticism or worry, and deception-detection self-efficacy conditioned skepticism but not trust or worry. Higher confidence in detecting deception predicted greater skepticism, suggesting that perceived evaluative competence can intensify scrutiny rather than foster trust. Drawing on experimental evidence from the high-stakes, underexamined context of cancer vaccines, this study advances understanding of trust formation in digital science communication by showing that message truthfulness and source credibility operate through distinct processing routes: systematic evaluation of content and heuristic reliance on source cues, respectively. The findings offer theoretically grounded guidance for practitioners and policymakers seeking to counter misinformation and strengthen public confidence in emerging biomedical innovations.

item.title: “It’s not punishment; it’s for their own good”: A positioning analysis of compassion in parole work
item.dc:creator: Chandler T. Marr, Alaina C. Zanin
item.description:
Communication Monographs · Chandler T. Marr, Alaina C. Zanin

Topics: Compassion, Discourse analysis, Positioning theory, Ethnography

Compassion is often assumed to be an unequivocally positive phenomenon that naturally yields generative outcomes such as healing, empowerment, and connection. This study challenges that assumption by demonstrating how compassion functions as a form of discipline. Drawing on over 100 hours of ethnographic fieldwork within a state corrections department and interviews with parole officers (n = 12) and administrators (n = 5), we identified three positioning strategies that officers utilized to recognize, relate, and (re)act to suffering: (a) culpable positioning, (b) sanctimonious positioning, and (c) paternalistic positioning. While these positioning strategies appear coercive, officers (re)interpreted them as necessary acts of support that guide supervisees toward rehabilitation. These findings extend compassion scholarship by resituating compassion as an ambiguous, occasionally disciplinary discursive process.

item.title: Between Watchdogs and Disseminators of Facts: Exploring How Spanish Journalists and Fact-checkers Perceive Their Roles Amidst Disinformation
item.dc:creator: Berta Olivier Cañadell, Michael Hameleers
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Berta Olivier Cañadell, Michael Hameleers

Topics: Journalistic roles, Fact-checking, Disinformation, Journalistic practice

Although journalists and fact-checkers are expected to flag disinformation and point news users to trustworthy content, we know little about whether they feel empowered to fulfil these expectations. Building upon previous research on journalistic role perceptions in the context of disinformation, this study investigates how Spanish journalists and fact-checkers perceive their roles. The analysis of in-depth semi-structured interviews with 18 journalists and fact-checkers reveals that these professionals strongly advocate for their role as disseminators, interpreters, and watchdogs, emphasizing their unique commitment to delivering reliable information to empower citizens. However, a significant disparity exists between the two groups. While fact-checkers are dedicated to actively fighting disinformation and promote media literacy, journalists in mainstream media face difficulties in fulfilling basic journalistic functions due to the competitive media landscape and high pressure to increase revenue, compounded by the fragile economic structures of their organizations. As a major implication for journalism practice, this study shows that although media practitioners are willing to engage in fact-checking, there needs to be more support and awareness about their roles as watchdogs of truth.

item.title: Beyond the Habermas machine: rethinking the democratic meaning of AI-assisted deliberation
item.dc:creator: Seong Jae Min
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Seong Jae Min

Topics: Artificial intelligence, Political communication, Communication theory, Digital democracy

Advances in artificial intelligence have generated renewed interest in using computational systems to facilitate democratic deliberation at scale. While recent efforts, exemplified by the ‘Habermas Machine,’ promise efficiency, balance, and consensus, they raise fundamental questions about the meaning of deliberation itself. This article offers a theoretical critique of deliberation using AI, focusing on systems that operationalize deliberation as a consensus-optimizing procedure. Drawing on Habermasian theories of communicative rationality, deliberative systems scholarship, and distinctions between private and public deliberation, the article argues that current AI approaches risk translating deliberation from communicative rationality into computational rationality. This shift privileges public acceptability and formal balance over critical contestation, reflexivity, and democratic legitimacy. In response, the article reconceptualizes AI-mediated communication by foregrounding private, informal interaction as a ‘pre-public’ space within the deliberative system, where citizens can explore disagreement in judgement-free context and develop deliberative capacities.

item.title: The Matthew Effect of Social Media Algorithms: News Avoidance and Polarisation of News Consumption
item.dc:creator: Rasmus W. Schmøkel, Kim Viborg Andersen, Morten Skovsgaard
item.description:
Digital Journalism · Rasmus W. Schmøkel, Kim Viborg Andersen, Morten Skovsgaard

Topics: Social media algorithms, News avoidance, News consumption, Political polarization

This study examines the dynamics of news consumption on social media platforms, focusing on how news avoidance motivations interact with algorithm-driven curation to potentially polarise news consumption. Using a novel experimental platform that mimics a social media news feed with a learning-based recommendation algorithm, we conducted a four-wave field experiment with repeated measures. The findings reveal that the interplay between news avoidance motivations and algorithmic influence results in a widening gap in news consumption between users with high and low levels of unintentional news avoidance, but not between users with high and low levels of intentional news avoidance. These results underline the important role of social media algorithms in generating information deficits among people with higher preference for entertainment than for news. Thereby, the study also demonstrates how experimental social media platforms can illuminate the opaque influence of algorithms, revealing otherwise hidden and inaccessible communication dynamics in today’s hybrid media environment.

item.title: Sentiment polarity and risk amplification in online public opinion: A configurational analysis of university crisis events
item.dc:creator: 乔玉为, Huiting Wang, Xinlong Xu
item.description:
Communication Monographs · 乔玉为, Huiting Wang, Xinlong Xu

Topics: Crisis communication, Social media discourse, Public opinion, Risk perception

Online public sentiment can shift rapidly during university crises, with consequences for institutional governance. Using fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) of 50 university crisis events in China, this study examines how public opinion object, response timeliness, event category, event influence, and school tier combine to shape event-level sentiment valence. Three configurations are associated with comparatively favorable sentiment outcomes: student-centered resonance, media-leveraged responsiveness, and structure-synchronized reputation. Complementary regression analyses identify response timeliness and event category as the most consistent net correlates, while school tier matters in conjunction with other conditions. By integrating configurational and regression evidence, the study extends crisis-communication research on sentiment dynamics and risk amplification and offers a pathway-based framework for institutional response.

item.title: Authority Over Sympathy: How AI Emotional Tone and Thinking Dispositions Shape Hallucination Detection in Health Communication
item.dc:creator: Lu Liu, Bing Hu
item.description:
Journal of Broadcasting & Electronic Media · Lu Liu, Bing Hu

Topics: Health communication, Generative AI, Misinformation, Information credibility

Drawing on the Misinformation Recognition and Response Model (MRRM), this study investigates how AI emotional tone and thinking dispositions influence hallucination detection in health communication. A Wizard-of-Oz experiment (N = 476) examined the role of authoritative and sympathetic tones as independently manipulated tone in AI-generated health responses containing embedded hallucinations. The results showed that authoritative tone significantly reduced participants’ hallucination detection sensitivity. While sympathetic tone did not show a significant effect. The analysis also indicated that thinking dispositions did not significantly moderate the influence of tone on hallucination detection sensitivity.

item.title: Towards an Adaptive Turn in Journalism: Conceptualizing the Algorithmic Co-Constitution of the News Media–Audience Relationship
item.dc:creator: Jannie Møller Hartley, Liisa Ovaska
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Jannie Møller Hartley, Liisa Ovaska

Topics: Algorithmic curation, Journalism, News production, Audience engagement

In this article, we introduce the term “adaptive turn” in the field of journalism to encapsulate the shift brought about by the introduction of algorithmic systems, such as predictive audience analytics, recommender systems, and generative AI technologies, across the news media industries. These algorithmic systems enable real-time adaptation to users’ individualized needs and actions based on their previous news consumption patterns. Previous literature and theorizing have dealt with either algorithmic systems focusing on the impact on journalistic values or practices or on the users’ algorithmic experiences, while our aim with the introduction of “the adaptive turn” is to conceptualize how these developments transform the relationship between the two separate fields. Building on an STS theoretical framework of technologies as mediating between humans and the world, we argue that the adaptive turn captures this shift to what we term the algorithmic co-constitution of the media/user relationship. By analysing current examples from existing literature, this paper pinpoints how this algorithmic co-constitution happens along four dimensions, namely a material, a normative, a commercial, and an epistemic dimension. Building on this, we suggest four research commitments going forward, which can qualify the identification of the social implications of the adaptive turn in journalism.

item.title: Generational differences in responses to disinformation: from ‘vulnerability’ to interpretive strategies
item.dc:creator: Stefan Janjić, Sabina Mihelj, Hanna Orsolya Vincze
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Stefan Janjić, Sabina Mihelj, Hanna Orsolya Vincze

Topics: Disinformation, Generational differences, Focus groups, Media literacy

Generational differences in responses to disinformation have attracted considerable attention, yet are rarely comprehensively theorised and are often examined with the help of surveys or behavioural data designs. Such designs tend to frame audience engagement from the perspective of ‘vulnerability’ or ‘resilience’ and offer limited insight into how audiences interpret and negotiate contested claims in everyday communication. In this article, we develop a more elaborated conceptualisation of generational differences and propose to understand disinformation not as a set of factual errors to be corrected but as a communicative practice that involves interpretation and interaction. We then examine generational differences in responses to disinformation in three European countries: Serbia, Poland, and Romania. Drawing on 18 focus groups conducted in April-May 2025, we analyse discussions prompted by four disinformation examples per country, two related to the war in Ukraine and two related to LGBTQ issues. We distinguish between three main types of interpretive arguments: those anchored in textual and presentational cues, those drawing on prior knowledge, and those that move toward broader associative narratives. We show that younger participants rely more on text-based scrutiny, older participants more often reframe the materials through personal experience and wider moral and political narratives, while middle-aged groups sit in between. This suggests that generational differences cannot be reduced to differences in susceptibility or media literacy but are grounded in different approaches to argumentation and interpretation.

item.title: Smartphones, Peer Relationships, and Depressive Symptoms: A Six-Year Growth Model of Adolescent Mental Health
item.dc:creator: Yoojin Chung, Peter Johannes Schulz, Yun‐Jung Choi, Ah-Jung Yang
item.description:
Media Psychology · Yoojin Chung, Peter Johannes Schulz, Yun‐Jung Choi, Ah-Jung Yang

Topics: Adolescent mental health, Smartphone use, Peer relationships, Longitudinal study

From a media psychology perspective, understanding how digital behaviors influence mental health requires attention to individual differences and changes over time. This study examined longitudinal associations among smartphone use, peer relationships, and depressive symptoms using six waves of the Korean Children and Youth Panel Survey 2018 (KCYPS 2018), a nationally representative panel of South Korean adolescents (N = 2,460; ages 10–15). Multilevel growth modeling distinguished between- and within-person components of smartphone use and peer relationships. Higher average smartphone use and within-person increases in smartphone use were associated with higher depressive symptoms. More positive peer relationships were associated with lower depressive symptoms at both levels. Although within-person fluctuations in peer relationships did not consistently moderate the association between within-person smartphone use and depressive symptoms, this moderating role changed over time. Specifically, more positive-than-usual peer relationships showed an increasingly pronounced buffering pattern in this association across adolescence. Gender differences were also observed: girls reported higher baseline depressive symptoms, whereas boys showed steeper increases over time. These findings demonstrate the importance of distinguishing between- and within-person processes and considering adolescents’ social contexts when examining associations between smartphone use and mental health.

item.title: Does Office Type Determine Gendered Campaign Messages?
item.dc:creator: Tae Hyun Lim, Yu Jeong Hwang
item.description:
Political Communication · Tae Hyun Lim, Yu Jeong Hwang

Topics: Political communication, Gender differences, Election campaigns, Content analysis

This study examines how candidates’ gender shapes campaign messaging across different branches and levels of political office. Prior research offers mixed evidence on whether women are more likely than men to emphasize communal traits and women-related policies, often because gender effects are examined without fully accounting for institutional context. We address this inconsistency by foregrounding the role of electoral institutions. Building on strategic stereotype theory, we argue that gendered campaign messaging is a strategic response to office-specific incentives and expectations. In particular, we expect gendered appeals to be more prevalent at lower levels of government than at higher levels, and more pronounced in legislative than in executive races. We test these expectations using an original dataset of 46,966 official campaign booklets issued by all candidates competing for district-based executive and legislative offices in seventeen national and local elections in South Korea from 2000 to 2022. These booklets are legally standardized, page-limited documents distributed to voters and provide a rare opportunity to compare campaign messages across offices while holding the communication medium constant. We measure gendered messaging through candidates’ use of relational language and women-related policy terms. The results show that female candidates emphasize relational identities and women’s policy concerns more than male candidates. Crucially, the magnitude of this gender gap varies across institutional contexts. Gender differences are larger in legislative contests than in executive races and increase as elections move from national to subnational levels.

item.title: The work of digital inclusion: exposing the digital labour of community workers fostering digital participation
item.dc:creator: Peta Robyn Mitchell, Amber Marshall, Kim Osman
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Peta Robyn Mitchell, Amber Marshall, Kim Osman

Topics: Digital inclusion, Digital labor, Digital divide, Digital literacy

This article presents findings from a national-scale research project that worked with disadvantaged communities across Australia to examine digital inclusion in low-income families and the role of social infrastructure (e.g., schools, libraries, charities, government services) in supporting digital participation. Drawing on data collected in interviews and community workshops in an outer urban community with significant socio-economic challenges, we illuminate the digital labour of community sector workers who routinely act as digital mentors. These workers support family members who often lack access to digital devices and services along with the requisite skills to use digital technologies to perform everyday tasks, such as helping families to contact telecommunications providers, access government apps, and apply for jobs or rental leases online. In light of our results, our study extends the concept of digital labour to include work undertaken in the service and advocacy of digital inclusion in community contexts. Specifically, we articulate the activities, challenges, frustrations, and costs (in time and resources) that characterise digital inclusion support of low-income families, often beyond role expectations. In doing this, we seek to expand understandings of digital labour both as a category and concept. Overall, the article demonstrates that digital inclusion initiatives must not only accommodate the intersecting socio-cultural needs of low-income families, but include appropriate support and resourcing for community workers performing critical digital mentoring work.

item.title: Narratives of transparency: how do commercial and non-commercial providers of research information legitimize the datafication of research?
item.dc:creator: Stella Köchling, Anne K. Krüger
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Stella Köchling, Anne K. Krüger

Topics: Academic publishing, Datafication, Digital infrastructure, Research information systems

The datafication of research has immensely expanded the possibilities for creating more metadata regarding research practice and performance. This has supported the growth of research information produced by commercial and non-commercial providers based on digital infrastructures including bibliometric databases, research information systems, and analytics services for the scientific community and beyond. In this paper, we ask how the providers of research information legitimize the need for the datafication of research and thus for their tools by looking at the providers’ narratives of transparency and how they differ according to their business model. Based on 22 expert interviews with employees of commercial and non-commercial organizations, we show that there are three narratives – demonstrating research performance, improving research, and supporting research governance – that build on distinct meanings of transparency, implying particular understandings of research practice and performance, which influence how research is made accessible and assessable through the metadata and analytics services the organizations provide.

item.title: Exploring Geographic “Reach” in Local Visual News: A Mapping Approach
item.dc:creator: T.J. Thomson, Kristy Hess, Rachael Anderson, Seraina Tarnutzer
item.description:
Journalism Studies · T.J. Thomson, Kristy Hess, Rachael Anderson, Seraina Tarnutzer

Topics: Visual journalism, Local news, Geographic mapping, Digital journalism

The importance of local news outlets having a physical presence in and understanding of the geographic places they serve is widely established in academic literature. Yet vast and sparsely populated coverage areas—such as those in regional, rural, or remote Australia—can challenge the feasibility and practicality of this ideal. This study explores the use of mapping methods to visualise and assess geographic patterns of visual news coverage published by two news outlets in communities in two different states, focusing on photographs as spatially anchored indicators of journalistic presence and attention. Specifically, we identify the locations of 701 news photographs published across the two outlets over a constructed year and then plot these on maps using a point-based approach. We then experiment with different ways of mapping these locations and reflect on the challenges of these approaches. In doing so, we highlight the value of using heat maps to more clearly reveal disparities in coverage density across the outlets’ self-defined “news zones”. Our findings demonstrate both the potential and limitations of mapping approaches in identifying under-served areas and in complicating the issue of a news outlet’s “geographic” reach in the digital era.

item.title: The few, the loud: platform-mediated articulation of conspiratorial discourse by political elites on X and Facebook
item.dc:creator: Piotr Marczyński, Nathalie Brack
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Piotr Marczyński, Nathalie Brack

Topics: Conspiracy theories, Political communication, Social media, Populism

Despite growing concerns about the role of political elites in producing and amplifying conspiracy theories, little is known about which politicians engage in this behavior, how prevalent it is across countries and platforms, and what ideological patterns it follows. We address these questions by identifying a narrow set of elite conspiracy entrepreneurs who disproportionately produce conspiratorial discourse, challenging the bounds of acceptable debate across three European democracies. Using gradient threshold analysis, logistic regression, and close reading, we analyze a manually annotated sample of posts by political elites (N = 702) in Belgium, Finland, and Poland to identify conspiracy entrepreneurs, characterize them, and examine their cross-platform communication. Results indicate that conspiratorial discourse is driven by a narrow set of predominantly far-right politicians, who generate higher engagement than their colleagues, despite comparable following and posting rates. Conspiratorial discourse also differs across platforms, with Facebook enabling more fully articulated conspiratorial narratives and X favoring more fragmented, context-dependent communication. These findings illuminate how political elites cultivate epistemic crisis and how social media platforms may algorithmically reward conspiratorial content by providing tools for politicians to generate engagement.

item.title: Interdependent Autonomy: How Digital-Native Media Adapt to Compound Constraints in Flawed Democracies
item.dc:creator: Kevin Alexis García, Javier Díaz-Noci, Laura Pérez-Altable
item.description:
Digital Journalism · Kevin Alexis García, Javier Díaz-Noci, Laura Pérez-Altable

Topics: Digital journalism, Press freedom, Journalistic practice, News organizations

This study investigates how digital-native media adapt their practices, organizational models, and community relationships when operating under the compound constraints characteristic of flawed democracies. Using a mixed-methods design structured around a case study of La Silla Vacía and Colombiacheck, two Colombian digital-native media outlets, the research integrates a mapping of 46 outlets in the Colombian digital ecosystem, content analysis of 701 articles published by both outlets (189 in depth), and 18 interviews with media ecosystem actors. The analysis identifies four interrelated adaptive dimensions, structural, methodological, territorial-digital, and relational, that respond to specific tensions between immediacy and rigor, digital reach and territorial presence, editorial independence and financial sustainability, and community engagement and journalistic objectivity. These dimensions converge in the concept of interdependent autonomy, the central theoretical contribution: editorial independence is preserved not despite but through the strategic diversification of alliances with other media, academia, civil society, and international cooperation. The findings demonstrate that in flawed democracies adaptation operates as a constitutive process, where compound constraints catalyze innovations that transcend the Colombian context for the understanding of journalism under democratic fragility globally.

item.title: Local in Name Only? The Impact of Ownership and Newsroom Proximity on Local and Original News Coverage
item.dc:creator: Simona Bisiani, Sarah Stonbely, Bahareh Rahmanzadeh Heravi
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Simona Bisiani, Sarah Stonbely, Bahareh Rahmanzadeh Heravi

Topics: News organizations, Journalism studies, Local news, Media systems

Local news plays a crucial democratic role by representing communities and reporting on place-based issues. Yet structural shifts such as chain ownership and the consolidation of local newsrooms risk diluting this local focus and increasing reliance on duplicated content. This study presents the first national analysis of local news authenticity in the UK using 465,105 articles from 360 outlets (2020–2022). We operationalise authentic localness using measures of geographic fidelity, coverage distance, and content duplication, and model how these vary by ownership and newsroom proximity. Our results show that corporate ownership reduces geographic fidelity and content originality, while increasing coverage distance, and that newsroom distance compounds this. Our findings demonstrate that ownership consolidation and newsroom centralisation jointly disembed journalism from communities, transforming local news from place-based reporting into networked content production.

item.title: The Democratic Cost of Pursuing Virality: A Study into Parliamentary Communications
item.dc:creator: André K. Rodarte
item.description:
Political Communication · André K. Rodarte

Topics: Political communication, Social media use, Mediatization, Political polarization

The transformation of parliamentarians into media producers has heightened concerns about emerging forms of political communication. This mixed-methods paper examines the strategies they employ to enhance their digital presence. Based on in-depth interviews, it shows that Brazilian parliamentarians believe that social media penalize them for posting about congressional matters, reporting that content about legislative work and constituency services receives little engagement online. Conversely, they view the production of antagonistic content and alignment with news cycles as essential to maintaining an engaging social media presence. A computational analysis of 4,5 million posts on Facebook, Instagram, and Twitter supports these evaluations: posts about congressional matters are associated with lower engagement metrics, while the use of antagonistic language increases them. The analysis further discusses pathways through which visibility is sustained at the intersection of platform incentives and communicative practices. In sum, this mixed-methods study demonstrates that the mediatization of politics has created perverse incentives for parliamentarians to downplay congressional activity and prioritize confrontations on social media, weakening accountability in ways that may resonate far beyond Brazil.

item.title: Weapon and poison? Framing disinformation in European Commission Speeches, 2016–2024
item.dc:creator: Eliana Fattorini, Alberto Acerbi, Massimiano Bucchi, Enzo Loner
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Eliana Fattorini, Alberto Acerbi, Massimiano Bucchi, Enzo Loner

Topics: Disinformation, Political communication, Platform governance, Media literacy

Drawing on 238 speeches delivered by European Commission (EC) presidents, vice-presidents, and commissioners (2016–mid-2024), this paper examines how the EC narrates ‘disinformation’. Using topic modelling, text-community detection, and qualitative content analysis, we show a generally self-absolving and fatalistic framing. Disinformation is considered the root cause of unwanted behaviours and events, naturalized as a technological inevitability given citizen gullibility. Moreover, responsibility for the spread of disinformation is externalized to hostile States, ‘bad actors’, and digital platforms. Battlefield and contagion metaphors (‘fight/weapon’; ‘poison/infodemic’) underpin a discursive policy repertoire focused on platform governance, detection/takedown, and media-literacy ‘vaccines’, positioning citizens as vulnerable subjects. Temporal analysis traces shifts from Russia-centred attributions to a broadened cast (China, Lukashenko) and, by 2023–2024, AI-enabled amplification. We argue that this framing narrows problem definitions and answers, imposing top-down solutions instead of supporting democratic dialogue. A better balance would combine fair platform rules with transparency, media pluralism, and participatory channels that treat citizens as interlocutors, so policies are shaped by informed dialogue rather than by presumptions of actors being misinformed.

item.title: Amplification, Contestation, and Toxic Interactions with Protest News: How Social Upheaval Reshapes Dynamics between News Organisations and Their Audiences
item.dc:creator: Ximena Orchard, Bastián González‐Bustamante, Carla Cisternas
item.description:
Digital Journalism · Ximena Orchard, Bastián González‐Bustamante, Carla Cisternas

Topics: Protest coverage, Audience engagement, Social media, News organizations

This study examines audience-media relations in the context of protest coverage, testing how dynamics of news media amplification and contestation in social media compare between legacy and alternative media. Empirically, we use difference-in-differences models to analyse the effects of the 2019 Chilean protests and a subsequent political agreement on audience-media interactions. Additionally, we probe such interactions as spaces for the expression of negative emotions, directed to media outlets as toxic replies. To this end, we apply pre-trained machine learning models to identify toxicity in user comments. Our dataset includes over 21 million posts mentioning 22 Chilean news organisations during a six-month period spanning three months before and after the protests. The findings show overall increased interactions with both media types after the outbreak of the protests, with distinct patterns of response: alternative media was more amplified while legacy media was more contested, reflecting on broader patterns of public media criticism. These results underscore the audience-media dynamic as a foundational element in how protests are portrayed and collectively interpreted.

item.title: Revisiting Framing Codebooks with AI: Employing Large Language Models as Analytical Collaborators in Deductive Content Analysis
item.dc:creator: Diego Gómez-Zará, Hernan Valdivieso, Jorge Pérez, Denis Parra, Sebastián Valenzuela
item.description:
Digital Journalism · Diego Gómez-Zará, Hernan Valdivieso, Jorge Pérez, Denis Parra, Sebastián Valenzuela

Topics: Large Language Models, News framing, Content analysis, Research methodology

Codebooks are central to framing research, providing theoretically grounded criteria for analyzing news content. While traditionally codebooks are built from theoretical frameworks and researchers' knowledge, applying these codebooks to large news corpora often exposes ambiguities, borderline cases, and underspecified rules that are difficult to resolve through theory alone. Moreover, news corpora evolve over time and differ across cultures, necessitating that researchers revisit the theoretical frameworks underlying these codebooks. In this article, we propose a workflow that uses Large Language Models (LLMs) to augment the creation and refinement of framing codebooks by combining theoretical frameworks with data-driven exploration. Rather than treating LLMs as automated classifiers, this approach positions them as analytic collaborators that help externalize decision rules, surface latent dimensions, and support iterative revisions of codebooks through dialogues between researchers and their data. We illustrate this workflow using a dataset of Latin American news coverage, demonstrating how the application of LLMs' capabilities has led to the surfacing of latent patterns, the generation of frame distinctions, and the adaptation of frameworks to new contexts. This method provides an LLM-assisted strategy that supports methodology creativity while preserving researchers' interpretative authority.

item.title: Do Your Own Research: What Skepticism of Expertise Means for the News Media in the U.S.
item.dc:creator: Ariel Hasell, Sedona Chinn
item.description:
Political Communication · Ariel Hasell, Sedona Chinn

Topics: Media trust, News consumption, Political polarization, Misinformation

In the U.S. the availability of news information has grown exponentially while trust in traditional sources of news and information has declined. Amid this high-information, low-trust environment, many now advocate for doing your own research (DYOR) to discern accurate claims from false, misleading, or biased information. The perception that it is better to do one’s own research has important implications for information seeking and attitudes toward mainstream news and journalism. In this study, we use a panel survey to investigate DYOR perceptions in the context of the 2020 U.S. election. We find that DYOR perceptions are associated with decreased nonpartisan news use, decreased belief accuracy, and more negative attitudes toward media, highlighting how information skepticism may be contributing to adversarial views toward mainstream media and expertise. Results suggest that such perceptions encourage negative views of news media and may contribute to distrust of public institutions.

item.title: Visibility, Power, and the Battle for Truth in an AI Age
item.dc:creator: T.J. Thomson, Ryan J. Thomas, Shangyuan Wu, Iuliia Alieva
item.description:
Digital Journalism · T.J. Thomson, Ryan J. Thomas, Shangyuan Wu, Iuliia Alieva

Topics: Visual journalism, Generative AI, Visibility and power, Misinformation

Visual journalism has always been a subjective practice involving questions of power. Whether conveyed through photographs, videos, illustrations, or as data, visual journalism is the process of making some elements more visible and others less so. The means by which this happens and how certain people, topics, or events are shown and represented carries symbolic and political weight. Hence, the link between visibility and power cannot be overstated. The contributions to this special issue examine how technological change is reshaping the forms, practices, power relations, and epistemic foundations of visual journalism. The special issue pushes back against logocentrism, considers how algorithms and GenAI are expanding the gaze, and reflects on the contours of the scholarly field and on how the changing nature and forms of visuals are affecting visual style and representational patterns. It also centres power as inseparable from the making, use, and manipulation of visuals. Ultimately, this special issue ponders the implications of not being able to trust our eyes, and muses about the epistemic crisis GenAI has created, which might harm our vision of a shared reality, more broadly, and the production and reception of visual news, in particular.

This study examines how recommendation systems organize differential news visibility on Douyin, one of China’s largest short-video platforms. Focusing on the visibility dynamics between government-affiliated media and non-government-affiliated media, the study adopts an agent-based testing (ABT) approach to audit how Douyin’s recommendation system allocates exposure under different stages of user interaction and preference formation. The findings suggest that government-affiliated media receive greater visibility during the early stages of recommendation, when user behavioral data remain limited. However, as recommendation systems accumulate interaction signals over time, non-government-affiliated media gradually gain visibility, particularly under conditions of sustained user engagement. At the same time, the recommendation system does not respond symmetrically to different forms of user preference, revealing varying degrees of algorithmic responsiveness in the visibility allocation process. By examining how recommendation systems negotiate commercial, institutional, and behavioral priorities in news distribution, this study contributes to research on algorithmic visibility, platform governance, and algorithm audit.

item.title: Do Emotional Ads Persuade? Evidence from Real-Time Campaign Advertising Experiments
item.dc:creator: John Murphy, Alexander Coppock, Seth J. Hill, Lynn Vavreck
item.description:
Political Communication · John Murphy, Alexander Coppock, Seth J. Hill, Lynn Vavreck

Topics: Political advertising, Persuasion, Political polarization, Election campaigns

We evaluate whether campaign advertisements that generate larger emotional reactions also generate larger persuasive effects in contemporary elections. We analyze 29 weeks of experiments conducted during the 2016 U.S. presidential campaign, in which 48 authentic campaign ads were tested in real time, often within days of their debut. The ads and a placebo were randomly assigned to approximately 28,000 subjects. We find that campaign ads reliably move emotions, albeit in largely partisan ways, with comparatively muted reactions among independents. Critically, however, these emotional reactions do not predict the magnitude of an ad’s effect on candidate favorability, vote intention, policy preferences, or turnout intention. Our results cast doubt on emotion-based accounts of advertising persuasion in polarized elections and caution practitioners against using self-reported emotional reactions as a measure of message effectiveness.
