Journalism Studies · Nando Malmelin, Matti Pihlajamaa, Sari Virta, Johanna Strandholm

Topics: Journalism, Organizational communication, Digital transformation, News production

News media organisations are under constant pressure to innovate and renew themselves. Under these conditions, intrapreneurship offers a way to advance innovation from within existing organisations by enabling employees to initiate, develop, and promote new ideas as part of their everyday work. This article examines how intrapreneurial practices support innovation in journalism and media work. Drawing on a practice-based, multi-level framework, the study analyses intrapreneurial activity at individual, team, and organisational levels in two Finnish news media companies. Based on a dual-case study of semi-structured interviews with media managers, the analysis examines concrete episodes that explain how intrapreneurial activity is initiated, advanced, and supported in journalism and media work. The findings show how intrapreneurial activity is enacted through interconnected practices across levels and depends on surrounding organisational conditions. The article offers a systematic way to analyse intrapreneurial activity in journalism and offers practical insights for news media professionals and organisations seeking renewal by showing how innovation is put into practice in everyday media work.

item.title: How Platform Affordances Shape Expression Effects: Comment Length and Audience in Political News Engagement
item.dc:creator: Jinping Wang, Liang Hai
item.description:
Journal of Broadcasting & Electronic Media · Jinping Wang, Liang Hai

Topics: Platform affordances, Political news engagement, Affective polarization, Social media affordances

This experiment (N = 775) examined how commenting affordances shape expression effects in political news. Participants were assigned to conditions that varied comment length (short vs. long) and audience type (private, public, ingroup, or outgroup) on a simulated news platform. Composition and release affordances interacted rather than operating independently: short ingroup-directed comments were associated with less anger and greater enthusiasm, whereas longer private comments heightened affective polarization relative to public ones. A computational linguistic analysis revealed distinct word-use patterns across conditions. Findings establish the contingent structure of expression effects and advance a mass–interpersonal–intrapersonal framework, with implications for news platform design.

item.title: Publishers’ Power: The Influence of Ownership on the Framing of Dutch Media Concentration (2003–2022)
item.dc:creator: Doris Bukman, Olga Eisele, Kathleen Beckers, Mark Boukes, Ulrike Klinger
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Doris Bukman, Olga Eisele, Kathleen Beckers, Mark Boukes, Ulrike Klinger

Topics: Media concentration, Media ownership, News framing, Journalistic autonomy

Journalism operates in market-based systems, forcing news outlets to balance editorial autonomy with financial imperatives. This friction raises concerns about media owners’ influence on news content, particularly coverage directly tied to their financial interests, such as media mergers. To examine this influence, we conducted an inductive-then-deductive content analysis on news coverage of media mergers, assessing which justifying and criticizing frames appeared and whether their use differed when the outlet’s owner was involved in the merger. The analysis focused on the period between 2003 and 2022 in the Netherlands, where strong editorial safeguards coexist with high media concentration. Findings showed that reporting on media mergers focused primarily on who owns the media and why, rather than on broader implications for the news market. Outlets used significantly more justifying frames when covering mergers involving their owner compared to when the owner was not involved. No difference was found for criticizing frames. Furthermore, while the Dutch market became increasingly concentrated, recent mergers featured more justifying but not fewer criticizing frames. Similarly, outlets undergoing takeovers engaged in more justification, while criticism was unaffected. Overall, the results call for a reconsideration of the presumed resilience of journalistic autonomy against corporate pressures in democratic markets.

item.title: “When You Do Journalism in Uganda, You Instinctively Avoid Covering Certain Stories.” Journalistic Tales of Fear in an Era of Digital Authoritarianism
item.dc:creator: Stephen Ssenkaaba
item.description:
Digital Journalism · Stephen Ssenkaaba

Topics: Digital authoritarianism, Press freedom, Journalistic practice, Political interference

This study examines how mainstream journalists in Uganda perceive and respond to digital authoritarianism. Drawing on in-depth interviews with 14 reporters and editors, the study explores the socioeconomic, legal, and technological factors shaping these perceptions. Findings indicate that journalists view state deployment of digital technologies as a threat to press freedom, freedom of expression, and other fundamental rights. However, economic precarity, political interference in media ownership, and restrictive regulatory environments limit journalists’ ability to resist or circumvent digital repression. The study argues that socioeconomic and political considerations are central to understanding both the construction of digital authoritarianism and its impact on journalism in Uganda.

item.title: Adaptation Through Hiring: A Reconfiguration of Journalists’ Skills and Roles
item.dc:creator: Matthew S. Weber, Allie Kosterich
item.description:
Digital Journalism · Matthew S. Weber, Allie Kosterich

Topics: Journalism, Digital transformation, Computational methods, Data journalism

The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence and information communication technologies has profoundly disrupted traditional professional structures, transforming how journalistic work is organized and understood. This study examines how journalism has adapted to these technological shifts through the emergence of new job roles and skills. Drawing from a communicative perspective, the research frames job advertisements as organizational artifacts that signal adaptation and reconfiguration of professional boundaries. Using a longitudinal dataset from 2010 through 2020 encompassing more than 400,000 job postings across the U.S. media sector, this study employs computational text analysis and clustering to trace evolving patterns in job titles and skill requirements. Findings reveal a significant rise in computational and data-driven competencies including analytics, programming, and data science within journalism roles, suggesting the integration of technological expertise into the profession’s core identity. Results highlight how organizations discursively construct new professions and communicate adaptation in response to ongoing change. By analyzing job roles as sites of organizational meaning-making, this work contributes to understanding the adaptation of new skills into existing professions and offers insight into the broader dynamics of transformation in the digital age.

item.title: Pressured by the Comments? Chinese Journalists in the Face of Online Violence
item.dc:creator: Siyu Chen
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Siyu Chen

Topics: Online harassment, Journalism, Digital media, Journalistic practice

In the increasingly digital context of China’s public sphere, journalists frequently encounter online violence that threatens their professional autonomy, emotional wellbeing, and freedom of expression. Drawing on 20 semi-structured interviews with journalists representing a cross section of the Chinese media landscape, this study identifies four major types of online violence experienced by Chinese journalists: violence in response to alleged unprofessional behaviours, violence based on moral coercion, violence motivated by so-called “nationalism”, and gendered violence. Cultural norms, nationalist ideologies, and patriarchy emerge as key factors shaping and underpinning online violence. With regard to journalists’ coping strategies, these are found to include individualised and emotionally taxing approaches, such as silence, avoidance and contempt, while institutional support is either limited in its responsiveness or sometimes unavailable. This study provides an enhanced understanding of the role of online violence in shaping journalistic practice and coping strategies in a highly interactive and emotional digital media environment. The findings indicate that online violence driven by wider structural and cultural forces, is becoming an increasingly common informal control mechanism, undermining journalistic authority and autonomy and therefore the stability and sustainability of journalism itself.

item.title: Digital ID as surreptitious experimentation in the humanitarian-tech industry: an ethnography of a biometric pilot in a refugee camp in the Thailand-Myanmar border
item.dc:creator: Mirca Madianou, Charlotte Hill, Hayso Thako, Anonymous, Anonymous
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Mirca Madianou, Charlotte Hill, Hayso Thako, Anonymous, Anonymous

Topics: Digital identity, Humanitarian-tech industry, Biometric systems, Surveillance

This article focuses on a technological pilot involving a digital identity system that was introduced in the hospital of a refugee camp along the Thailand-Myanmar border. Drawing on an 18-month-long ethnographic study of refugees’ experiences with biometric systems, the article analyses the pilot as an example of ‘surreptitious experimentation’. Surreptitious experimentation is symptomatic of the wider commercialisation and digital infrastructuring of the humanitarian space, which we make sense of through the term ‘humanitarian-tech industry’. This is a mixed methods study involving semi-structured and group interviews, participatory art sessions and ethnography. In total, we spoke with 174 refugees and 27 expert participants involved in the aid operations. The research found that the digital ID system was implemented despite local misgivings. The term ‘surreptitious’ illustrates the fact that the new system was not announced as a ‘pilot’, but rather simply rolled out to replace existing forms of patient registration. Because the pilot took place in the infrastructural background, it remained hidden. The article documents the lack of local understanding and meaningful consent among refugees. The promise of ‘self-sovereign’ decentralised identity advocated by the pilot sponsors was never communicated to the local communities, let alone ever realised, even when a need for data portability emerged. Instead, the article observes that the pilot introduced harms and amplified the asymmetries which already exist in humanitarian and particularly medical humanitarian settings. As an exemplar of surreptitious experimentation, the digital ID pilot reworked and revitalised the colonial logics of aid.

item.title: The Evolution of Mainstream Media Clickbait on WeChat (2015–2024): A Longitudinal Analysis of Issue Distribution, Intermedia Homogenization, and Engagement Efficacy
item.dc:creator: Jinjin Zhou, Jingjun Wang, Ye Wu
item.description:
Digital Journalism · Jinjin Zhou, Jingjun Wang, Ye Wu

Topics: Social media platforms, News consumption, Media coverage, Audience engagement

item.title: Double Adaptation: Negotiating Closeness and Managing Boundaries in Journalist–Politician Relations
item.dc:creator: Marína Urbániková, Lenka Waschková Císařová, Iveta Jansová, Melanie Haberl, Folker Hanusch, Sophie K. Lecheler
item.description:
Digital Journalism · Marína Urbániková, Lenka Waschková Císařová, Iveta Jansová, Melanie Haberl, Folker Hanusch, Sophie K. Lecheler

Topics: Journalism studies, Political communication, Professional norms, Journalistic practice

Closeness with politicians is both a professional resource and a potential risk for journalists, as it enables access to information but may compromise autonomy and integrity, particularly within today’s hybrid media environment. This study proposes the conceptual framework of double adaptation as a sensitizing, process-oriented lens for a more systematic understanding of how journalists manage boundaries with politicians, drawing on 96 semi-structured interviews with political journalists in Austria and Czechia. Double adaptation captures the dual process through which journalists adjust their practices in response to both immediate situational demands and structural conditions. Boundaries in journalist–politician interactions emerge through situational adaptation to specific contexts, requiring a careful balancing across multiple dimensions of closeness. The analysis identifies nine such dimensions, grouped into two domains: interactions and relationships. The study further identifies individual factors shaping situational adaptation, including symbolic and pragmatic approaches to boundary management, and situational factors such as personal affinity. Simultaneously, boundaries result from structural adaptation operating at organizational, professional, and systemic levels, influenced by digital transformation, economic pressures, and the professionalization of political communication. Together, these insights advance a more systematic and processual conceptualization of boundary management in political journalism by linking everyday interactional practices to broader structural transformations.

item.title: Democratic Accountability in East Asia: A Comparative Experimental Study of Voter Responses to Norm Violations
item.dc:creator: Woo Chang Kang, Sunkyoung Park, Osbern Huang, Koh IWABUCHI, Tetsuro Kobayashi
item.description:
Political Communication · Woo Chang Kang, Sunkyoung Park, Osbern Huang, Koh IWABUCHI, Tetsuro Kobayashi

Topics: Political polarization, Public opinion, Persuasion, Political communication

Existing research shows that voters in established democracies often fail to penalize politicians who violate democratic norms, as many are willing to trade democratic principles for partisan interests in polarized environments. Yet such partisan double standards remain underexplored in East Asia, where countries share authoritarian legacies, face ongoing risks of democratic backsliding, and operate under the geopolitical shadow of powerful authoritarian neighbors. Using a large-scale vignette experiment conducted in Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and the United States (N = 10,194), this study examines whether voters sanction politicians who engage in democratic norm violations. We focus on reactions to three types of undemocratic statements: election denial, protest suppression, and attacks on the judiciary. The results show that voters in East Asian democracies impose stronger penalties than their American counterparts, though the degree and pattern of accountability differ across cases. Election denial consistently generates the strongest sanctions, while Japan and Taiwan show robust reactions across all scenarios. South Korea displays comparatively modest responses to protest suppression, and the United States shows the weakest effects overall. These findings highlight both the resilience and the heterogeneity of democratic accountability in East Asia and underscore the need to understand regional variation when assessing the prospects for democratic stability.

item.title: From #StayWoke to “Culture Wars”: How Social Justice Discourse is Separately and Synergistically Politicized on Twitter and YouTube
item.dc:creator: Sara Holland Levin, Rui Wang, J. Mira Seo, Yi Yin Leong, Emma Bennett, Dongdong Yang, Zhuohui Yang, Matt Chen, Yini Zhang, Jiyoun Suk
item.description:
Political Communication · Sara Holland Levin, Rui Wang, J. Mira Seo, Yi Yin Leong, Emma Bennett, Dongdong Yang, Zhuohui Yang, Matt Chen, Yini Zhang, Jiyoun Suk

Topics: Political polarization, Social media platforms, Social media discourse, Digital platforms

This paper explores how the discourse surrounding a racially marginalized community becomes politicized via culture war narratives across platforms. Drawing from identity politics and political polarization research, we discuss how racial justice discourse can be hijacked by partisan opinion leaders and their followers over time and explain how this process plays out through both differentiated and coordinated social media platform use. Situating our discussion in the “woke” discourse as originated within the Black Twitter community, we collect data from 2012 through 2022 on Twitter and YouTube and apply user- and content-level computational analyses. Results show that the term “woke” has been increasingly amplified in culture war conversations on both platforms over time. However, the two platforms exhibited differences: culture war topics dominated on Twitter, while conservative news and commentary channels were most prevalent on YouTube. These two platforms were also interrelated in the politicization process. YouTube was a top domain within external links embedded in tweets, and Twitter was also a top destination within the external links embedded in YouTube video descriptions. Conservatives were especially keen on sharing right-wing content across platforms, from YouTube to Twitter, suggesting the success of cross-platform coordination in amplifying culture wars. Both theoretical and political implications for polarization on social media are discussed.

item.title: Blindness and epistemic injustice: a critical autoethnography of digital disablement in Thailand
item.dc:creator: Quanchai Kerddaen
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Quanchai Kerddaen

Topics: Digital inequality, Digital divide, Artificial intelligence, Digital platforms

Thailand’s digital transformation is presented as a route to inclusion, yet everyday accessibility remains unresolved for many disabled people. Combining policy document analysis with critical autoethnography, grounded in emancipatory disability research and analysed through a narrative approach, this article examines nearly thirty years of my experience as a blind person navigating education, public administration, banking, telecommunications, digital platforms, and generative AI in Thailand. Four interlocking patterns emerge: inaccessible documents and interfaces, conditional banking and biometric access, dependence on everyday platforms, and generative AI as compensatory access and epistemic risk. I develop the cycle of digital disablement to explain how these patterns persist despite formal accessibility commitments. The cycle is reproduced through three mutually reinforcing mechanisms: socio-epistemic exclusion, which limits the institutional force of disabled people’s knowledge of inaccessibility; techno-epistemic ableism, which embeds normative assumptions about bodies, perception, competence, and verification in technical systems; and socio-techonomic disadvantage, a term combining the technological and the economic, which transfers the financial, temporal, cognitive, relational, and privacy costs of accessibility failure to disabled users. Policy documents reveal that formal rights are diluted through regulatory silence, voluntary standards, weak enforcement, institutional discretion, and competing priorities. The analysis also shows workarounds widening immediate access while concealing the inaccessible arrangements that necessitated them. The article contributes an integrated account of digital exclusion as an epistemic, technical, material, and regulatory condition. Digital justice therefore requires enforceable accessibility duties, non-visual authentication, accessible materials and interfaces, accountable AI governance, effective remedies, and disabled people’s authority in design, regulation, and evaluation.

item.title: Beyond beyond standardization: studying robustness of empirical claims based on topic modeling through multiverse analysis
item.dc:creator: Paul Balluff, Christina Viehmann, Maximilian Linde, Yannik Peters, Jun Sun, Chung‐hong Chan
item.description:
Communication Methods and Measures · Paul Balluff, Christina Viehmann, Maximilian Linde, Yannik Peters, Jun Sun, Chung‐hong Chan

Topics: Topic modeling, Computational text analysis, Research methodology, Robustness

While topic modeling is widely used, some scholars have already announced that the application of topic modeling in social science research is impossible to standardize. Meanwhile, researchers have to make numerous methodological decisions, yet base their empirical claims on just one topic model. This raises the question of robustness about those claims. In this study, we apply the framework of preregistered multiverse analysis to evaluate the robustness of previous empirical claims from six studies that were based on topic modeling. Based on the Open Science materials of these six studies, we slightly modify the original topic modeling procedures, such as preprocessing, number of topic clusters, and topic modeling algorithm, to other defensible choices and determine whether the empirical claims remain consistent. Even though we observe that certain empirical claims are more robust, most claims are distorted considerably by changes to the modeling options. The contributions of this study are twofold. First, we confirm that empirical claims based on just one topic model might not be robust against numerous researcher degrees of freedom. Second, we advocate a wider adoption of preregistered multiverse analysis in social science research for checking the robustness of empirical findings.

item.title: News is Becoming Similar? A Diachronic Text Mining Exploration of News Convergence in Chinese Media
item.dc:creator: Junheng Qian, Zhi-Jin Zhong
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Junheng Qian, Zhi-Jin Zhong

Topics: News convergence, Computational text analysis, News media, Audience engagement

The convergence of news has long been a central concern in media studies, yet empirical evidence and precise measurements remain limited. China’s unique media system, which operates simultaneously in domestic and global contexts under distinct communication strategies, offers a rare opportunity to advance this line of inquiry. This study draws on news posts (N = 607,871) from four leading Chinese outlets over the past decade and applies a text-mining approach to examine Chinese news convergence across the two contexts and its relationship with audience news engagement. The results show a significant increase in lexical similarity among Chinese media in the global context but not in the domestic context. No upward trend in thematic structural similarity is observed in either context. Moreover, the associations between convergence and audience engagement are context-dependent: in the domestic context, lexical similarity is negatively associated with engagement, whereas in the global context, both lexical and thematic similarity are positively associated with engagement. These results challenge conventional views of news convergence, highlighting its dynamic nature across temporal and contextual dimensions. Further implications for theory and practice are discussed.

item.title: Electoral targeting strategies during the 2022 election in Sweden: exploring the paid affordances of Facebook and Instagram
item.dc:creator: Andreas Widholm, Mattias Ekman, Anders Olof Larsson
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Andreas Widholm, Mattias Ekman, Anders Olof Larsson

Topics: Political advertising, Election campaigns, Platform affordances, Political communication

Social media platforms have become central arenas for political communication, yet research has primarily focused on organic content rather than paid advertising. This study examines how Swedish political parties utilized Facebook and Instagram's paid affordances during the 2022 parliamentary election, analyzing a census sample (N = 2395) of ads from Meta's ad library. Combining content analysis with data on campaign spending and demographic targeting, the study identifies key differences in advertising strategies. We find that right-wing opposition parties engaged in more negative campaigning than left-wing incumbents, while calls to action were infrequent overall. The Center Party, the Sweden Democrats, and the Moderate Party emerged as the highest campaign spenders. Targeting strategies varied: left-leaning parties primarily targeted their messages toward women, whereas right-leaning parties focused on older male users. These findings contribute to the understanding of evolving party communication strategies, highlighting the role of paid social media advertising in contemporary election campaigns.

item.title: From Victim to Mutual Helper: Identity Work in University Students’ Telecommunications Fraud Narratives on Xiaohongshu
item.dc:creator: Weishan Miao, Hongjun Zhu, Jiankun Gong, Yarong Chen, Yuqi Feng, Langqi Hu, Hanxin Shen
item.description:
Journal of Broadcasting & Electronic Media · Weishan Miao, Hongjun Zhu, Jiankun Gong, Yarong Chen, Yuqi Feng, Langqi Hu, Hanxin Shen

Topics: Social media, Social identity, Digital platforms, Misinformation

Telecommunications and online fraud have become significant risks to young people, yet less is known about how victims reconstruct identity after victimization. Drawing on the Communication Theory of Identity, this qualitative study analyzes 100 Xiaohongshu posts published by university student victims between 2022 and 2026. Findings identify four interrelated identity positions: victim, agent, reflective self, and mutual helper. Rather than forming a linear sequence, these positions coexist and overlap in a recursive process of identity work across personal, enacted, relational, and communal frames. Through public narration, victims acknowledge harm, reclaim agency, reinterpret deception, and convert suffering into anti-fraud knowledge and peer support. The study highlights the importance of destigmatization, post-victimization support, and victim voice in building more inclusive anti-fraud communities.

item.title: Satire in Exile: Exiled Newsfluencers' use of Satire as a Discursive Strategy
item.dc:creator: Chun Hong Tse, Tomás Dodds, Rosalynd Southern
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Chun Hong Tse, Tomás Dodds, Rosalynd Southern

Topics: Satire, Newsfluencers, Social media, Political communication

This article examines how one newsfluencer in exile employs satire as a discursive strategy to sustain counter-publics in autocratic contexts. Through a multimodal critical discourse analysis of twenty videos by Stephen Shiu, a prominent Hong Kong newsfluencer now based in Taiwan, this article identifies a range of satirical strategies used in his commentary, including irony, exaggeration, parody, mock expertise, profanity, insult, metaphor, rumour, and personal anecdote. Drawing from these findings, we discuss how, in this case, satirists in exile may help provide critical information when domestic journalism is silenced, articulate collective frustration through emotional expression, and preserve local Cantonese profanity as a form of identity politics. This article adds to the literature on satire and social media by showing that online platforms like YouTube provide newsfluencers in exile with greater freedom of expression than would have been possible in legacy media, as well as sustain critical journalism in exile.

item.title: Folk Theories of Journalistic Authority in the Wake of the 2024 Valencia Floods
item.dc:creator: Ruth A. Palmer, Vincent Doyle
item.description:
Digital Journalism · Ruth A. Palmer, Vincent Doyle

Topics: Journalistic authority, Social media criticism, Discourse analysis, TikTok

This paper uses discourse analysis to analyze folk theories of journalistic authority—that is, lay beliefs about when and why journalism should be listened to (Carlson, 2017)—that circulated on TikTok in the wake of catastrophic floods in 2024 in Valencia, Spain. Many citizens took to social media to criticize the institutional response to the crisis, including the news coverage. Our analysis of that media criticism reveals three folk theories of journalistic authority dominated this discourse: that journalists have a duty to tell the truth; a duty to hold political actors to account; and a duty to care for citizens in need. Our analysis further shows that TikTokers used these folk theories to construct their own authority—by showing that they themselves uphold these duties where professional journalists fall short—and do so in ways that comply with social media logics, thus generating engagement to the benefit of themselves and social media platforms, but at the expense of the journalistic authority of the mainstream news media.

item.title: Social Media Savvy? The Use and Effectiveness of Political Parties’ Issue Strategies Across Platforms in the German Federal Election Campaign 2025
item.dc:creator: Christoph Ivanusch, Simon M. Luebke, Anna-Katharina Wurst, Jörg Haßler
item.description:
Political Communication · Christoph Ivanusch, Simon M. Luebke, Anna-Katharina Wurst, Jörg Haßler

Topics: Political communication, Social media platforms, Political campaigns, Election campaigns

How does the ever-growing relevance of social media shape political campaigning? A vibrant public and academic debate addresses the role of social media in elections and democratic processes. Yet, despite a surge in research, we still know little about the extent to which political parties adjust established issue strategies to the priorities of different social media platforms’ audiences and how effective these are in generating user engagement. Drawing on theories of issue competition – issue ownership, riding-the-wave, and issue yield – we analyze parties’ social media communication during the 2025 German federal election campaign on Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok. Combining manual quantitative content analysis of party and candidate posts with large-scale survey data from the German Longitudinal Election Study (GLES), we assess both strategic use and effectiveness of issue strategies. Our results show that parties strategically prioritize owned issues and those salient on the general public agenda, often combining both dimensions in issue yield strategies. However, these strategies only partly align with what the specific platform audiences value and reward. User engagement is highest for posts that match platform-specific issue preferences, especially when the issues are salient both to a party’s supporters on that platform and to its wider user base. The findings offer new insights into the dynamics of contemporary digital campaigning and cross-platform party competition.

item.title: The accuracy of survey measures on political activity on Facebook. Evidence from a data donation study
item.dc:creator: Zoltán Kmetty, Ádám Stefkovics
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Zoltán Kmetty, Ádám Stefkovics

Topics: Political participation, Data donation, Measurement validity, Facebook

Self-reported survey measures of social media use are commonly used across disciplines, yet the validity of findings in this area depends heavily on the accuracy of these reports. In political communication research, measurement error in reported online political behavior can distort estimates of media effects and lead to misleading conclusions about online political engagement. To address this concern, our study leveraged donated digital trace data from 758 Hungarian Facebook users and compared it with responses to standard survey questions provided by the same individuals. In addition, in a pre-registered experiment, we varied the ordering of the survey items. Our findings reveal moderate correlations between self-reported and actual digital behavior. General items showed closer alignment with observed behavior than self-reports of specific political activities. Participants typically underestimated their general Facebook activities and overestimated their political engagement on Facebook. Importantly, some of this discrepancy may stem not from respondents’ inaccuracy but from difficulties in classifying digital actions as politically relevant. Survey measures were more reliable in the general-specific questionnaire design and among individuals with high political interest. We discuss potential avenues for improving survey-based measures and emphasize the need for further research to address the methodological challenges associated with the use of digital trace data.

item.title: Relationship Between News Media Trust and News Consumption of Mainstream and Non-Mainstream Sources
item.dc:creator: Azade Asadi Damavandi, Louisa S. Ha
item.description:
Journal of Broadcasting & Electronic Media · Azade Asadi Damavandi, Louisa S. Ha

Topics: Media trust, News consumption, News media, Social media news

This national survey of U.S. adults examines how trust in specific types of news media predicts the consumption of different news sources. The findings reveal that the relationship between media trust and news consumption differs across media types. Trust in national news media is positively associated with both national and local news consumption, but trust in local news media predicts only local news consumption and is unrelated to national news use. In contrast, trust in online-only news organizations and social media news shared by influencers and non-news organizations is associated exclusively with the consumption of non-mainstream news sources. These findings suggest that media trust is complex with distinct forms of trust by news media type, shaping different patterns of news use rather than reflecting a generalized orientation toward news. By examining trust at the media-type level, this study offers a more nuanced understanding of how audiences navigate an increasingly diverse multiplatform news environment and provides theoretical and practical insights into the role of trust in contemporary news consumption.

item.title: When politics shapes technology adoption: a cross-national study of chatbot acceptance
item.dc:creator: Hui Zhou, Genia Kostka
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Hui Zhou, Genia Kostka

Topics: Artificial intelligence, Technology adoption, Political polarization, Cross-cultural communication

Existing literature on chatbot acceptance has largely relied on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) or Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), often neglecting the broader political, cultural, and attitudinal factors that shape user perceptions. Drawing on a cross-national survey conducted across four countries, we confirm the explanatory power of TAM/UTAUT indicators, while uncovering new determinants rooted in political values and cross-national perceptions. Specifically, participants are more likely to accept chatbots originating from countries toward which they hold positive sentiments — a country-of-origin effect linked to evaluations of political systems and technological advancement. Moreover, political ideology and technological openness significantly influence acceptance levels, but privacy concerns play a surprisingly minor role, except that German and American respondents' concern about excessive data collection hinders the acceptance of chatbots. These findings suggest that chatbot adoption is not merely a matter of technological functionality but also of political perception and cultural trust.

item.title: Rethinking Assumptions About Moral Content Selection: Moral-Emotional Content May Be Less Appealing Than Assumed
item.dc:creator: Isabella Rebasso, Yanna Krupnikov
item.description:
Political Communication · Isabella Rebasso, Yanna Krupnikov

Topics: Moral-emotional content, Selective exposure, Political polarization, Social media

Recent work has shown that moral-emotional content spreads rapidly on social media platforms such as X (Twitter). These patterns have led to concerns that social media facilitates the spread of moral outrage – potentially exacerbating political conflict and animosity. While most past work has focused on the supply side of this phenomenon, i.e. the transmission of morally charged political content, we consider the demand side: do people actually want to see this type of content in their information environment? In this paper, we first theoretically contextualize the motivations to engage with or avoid moral-emotional content. Then, through three pre-registered studies conducted in the U.S. in 2022 and 2023, we test whether people actively choose information that includes moral-emotional elements. Contrary to our initial expectations, we find that participants do not actively select moral-emotional content compared to neutral or emotional content. Despite previous findings on transmission, our results suggest that people may not want to see this type of content in their information environment. By focusing on selection rather than transmission, the findings presented in this paper add another nuance to an ongoing debate on the prevalence and consequences of online political outrage.

item.title: Hold That Thought: Enhancing the Durability of Fact-Checking Effects Through Low-Cost Accuracy Reminders
item.dc:creator: Je Hoon Chae, Tim J. Groeling, Hyunjin Song
item.description:
Political Communication · Je Hoon Chae, Tim J. Groeling, Hyunjin Song

Topics: Fact-checking, Misinformation correction, Longitudinal study, Information processing

Prior evidence suggests that fact-checking can update beliefs regarding factually incorrect information in the short term but its effects often decay rapidly. Such decay raises normative concerns about its sustainability and real-world impact. Here, we examine whether a cognitively efficient, low-cost intervention – called an “accuracy reminder” – can enhance the durability of fact-checking effects. In a large-scale pre-registered panel longitudinal experiment (N = 7,188), participants were randomly assigned to receive fact-checks and, under some conditions, follow-up prompts to reevaluate the same claim at interval-optimized time points. Across topical domains and partisan identities, reminder conditions produced durable belief correction effects lasting up to four weeks, more than doubling the persistence observed without reminders. Effects were robust across reminder frequency and timing, as well as against individual differences, suggesting implementation flexibility and theoretical generalizability. These findings identify retrieval-based reinforcement as a scalable means of sustaining factual belief correction and reinforcing shared factual baselines in spite of cognitive decay and partisan resistance.

item.title: Calibration labour: making careers machine-legible under algorithmic hiring
item.dc:creator: Xin Zhan
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Xin Zhan

Topics: Algorithmic curation, Digital labor, Platform governance, Digital inequality

This article reconceptualises algorithmic hiring as a transformation in the communicative conditions of recruitment rather than primarily as a problem of decision-making. Drawing on two years of ethnographic fieldwork at a London-based employment agency and training programme, it examines how employability is produced when recruitment is mediated by AI-enhanced applicant tracking systems (ATS). The article introduces algorithmic legibility as a communicative regime through which candidates encounter evaluation via asymmetrical proxy signals – such as metrics, thresholds, and prolonged silence – rather than through dialogic explanation. It demonstrates how this shift transforms job seeking from an interpersonal imitation game rooted in socialised modelling into a rationalised calibration game that demands calibration labour: the iterative, individualised restructuring of CVs, timelines, and narratives to align with opaque infrastructural criteria. The article argues that this infrastructure reconfigures recruitment into a restrictive recognition game in which visibility is increasingly reserved for biographies that can be readily rendered machine-legible. Under these conditions, interpretive labour is redistributed downwards, institutions are relieved of explanatory accountability, and marginalised jobseekers are compelled to become technicians of their own datafied subjectivities. Beyond corporate selection, this shift erodes the status of employment as a locus of social recognition and civic participation, contributing to the production of the algorithmic citizen – a subject whose socio-political inclusion becomes increasingly contingent upon continuous machine legibility. Algorithmic hiring, the article argues, governs access to work not through selection alone, but by reshaping whose lives can be rendered recognisable, on what terms, and through what forms of labour.

item.title: Influence operations 2.0: the evolution of social media manipulation in Southeast Asia
item.dc:creator: Kris Ruijgrok, Ward Berenschot, Yatun Sastramidjaja, Fatima Gaw, Janjira Sombatpoonsiri, Wiyayanto, Mariam Jayne M. Agonos
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Kris Ruijgrok, Ward Berenschot, Yatun Sastramidjaja, Fatima Gaw, Janjira Sombatpoonsiri, Wiyayanto, Mariam Jayne M. Agonos

Topics: Influence operations, Social media manipulation, Disinformation, Digital platforms

Given the dynamic and constantly evolving character of domestic online influence operations (IO), more knowledge of how these operations are changing is critical for efforts to counter the corrosive effects of IO on democracy and public debate. This article analyses the evolution of IO in Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines, using interviews with individuals involved in executing such operations. We identify a five-fold transformation. First, we trace a shift from state-dominated influence campaigns to a broader spectrum of clients. Second, we observe increased outsourcing of the operational work to private companies and freelancers. Third, we find a shift from quantity to quality in social media accounts, with IO workers operating fewer, more carefully crafted and influential profiles, alongside more limited use of automated bots. Fourth, content strategies have matured: instead of simply echoing state narratives, contemporary IO use data analytics to craft content tailored to specific audiences, often through subtle reframing of news rather than blatant disinformation. Fifth, dissemination methods have similarly shifted – from overwhelming social platforms with content to a more responsive, targeted, and data-informed approach. These changes signal a move toward more refined and strategic influence tactics. We conclude by highlighting likely causes of these transformations, and discuss implications for efforts to counter IO.

item.title: “If No One Is Doing Anything, What’s the Point of Hearing about It Again and Again?” Youth, Climate Journalism and Mediated Public (Dis)connection
item.dc:creator: Ingerid Birgitte Solheim Salvesen
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Ingerid Birgitte Solheim Salvesen

Topics: Climate change communication, Journalism, Social media use, Political engagement

For news media, climate journalism has been identified as both a normative responsibility and a strategic beat for reaching young audiences. This paper examines whether and how news media shape engagement with and public connection to climate change among Norwegian youth. Drawing on an in-depth qualitative study of 33 participants in a high-choice, digitally advanced media environment, I analyse the place of climate journalism in everyday media repertoires of youth. Prior engagement is decisive: climate issues are salient for already-concerned youth, but largely absent among others. Across groups, news media are not primary sources for climate information or engagement, suggesting that news-centric audience research may overstate news media’s role in public engagement with climate change and overlook youth-specific media habits. Combining different mediated public connection frameworks, the study shows why news media often fail to connect young people to climate change as a public issue. It introduces two interrelated analytical concepts: a lack of spatiotemporally grounded solutions in news coverage, which can lead to informed disconnection, a form of public disconnection with climate change partly produced by, rather than resolved by, climate journalism. Further, it proposes practice-oriented recommendations.

item.title: Echoes across the divide: incivility and the fragmentation of issue publics in immigration discourse
item.dc:creator: Yiqi Li, Aimei Yang
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Yiqi Li, Aimei Yang

Topics: Political polarization, Online communities, Large Language Models, Social networks

As immigration remains one of the most polarizing issues in U.S. politics, public discourse around it has become increasingly uncivil, especially on social media. This longitudinal study examines how incivility spreads and escalates across ideologically opposed issue publics on X. Drawing on conflict spiral theory, we conceptualize incivility as both a symptom and a driver of deepening conflict between pro-and antiimmigration publics. Additionally, we consult insights from research on networked publics and networked social influence to understand how online interactions shape the diffusion of hostile rhetoric. Using largescale X data, we deploy large language models to classify users' immigration stances and measure linguistic incivility. We also construct dynamic mention networks and apply graph-based machine learning to trace how incivility spreads over time and across ideological boundaries. The findings illuminate how conflict dynamics manifest through group network structures and how networked interactions spread incivility across groups with different immigration stances.

item.title: Generational warfare online? Social media use and intergroup attitudes in a national survey
item.dc:creator: Andrew M. Lindner, Elena O'Connell
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Andrew M. Lindner, Elena O'Connell

Topics: Social media use, Intergroup attitudes, Algorithmic curation, Social media influencers

Content analyses document vitriolic generational discourse across social media platforms, yet surveys reveal moderate attitudes among the public. Does social media exposure create extreme generational attitudes? Using nationally representative survey data (n=1,221), this study examines whether total social media use and platform-specific usage patterns correlate with generational self-identification and intergroup attitudes among American adults. Results reveal limited associations with even frequent users not exhibiting greater generational antagonism. Platform-specific analyses reveal few significant effects, though YouTube use is associated with more favorable attitudes toward other generations. These largely null findings suggest extreme online discourse does not reflect typical users’ attitudes, implying that reasons for extreme discourse are connected to visibility mechanisms, such as algorithmic amplification and creators’ strategic performance. The study also demonstrates the risks of inferring population attitudes from content analysis.

item.title: Do actions speak louder? The primacy of verbal person-centeredness for patients with invisible illness
item.dc:creator: Danni Liao, Grace M. Hildenbrand, Jia Yan, Huai-yu Chen
item.description:
Communication Monographs · Danni Liao, Grace M. Hildenbrand, Jia Yan, Huai-yu Chen

Topics: Health communication, Supportive communication, Nonverbal communication, Emotion regulation

Guided by conversationally induced reappraisal and discrepant verbal–nonverbal profile theories, this study examines how verbal person-centeredness (VPC) and nonverbal immediacy jointly influence emotional outcomes for patients with invisible illnesses. In a 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 online experiment (N = 497), participants coping with anxiety or chronic pain received supportive messages varying in VPC, nonverbal immediacy, and source (health care provider vs. fellow patient). Structural equation modeling showed that high VPC had stronger indirect effects on emotional improvement via cognitive reappraisal and perceived goodwill than low VPC, regardless of support source. Nonverbal immediacy enhanced outcomes via perceived goodwill, but only when paired with high VPC, suggesting the primacy of verbal (in)validation in invisible illness contexts.

item.title: Survival Tactics: Investigative Journalism Methods Under Threats and Barriers in Kazakhstan
item.dc:creator: Shynggys Atay, Rimma Zhaxylykbayeva, M. Zhetpisbaeva, О.Ж. Ошанова, Lazıza Nurpeııs
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Shynggys Atay, Rimma Zhaxylykbayeva, M. Zhetpisbaeva, О.Ж. Ошанова, Lazıza Nurpeııs

Topics: Investigative journalism, Journalistic practice, Press freedom, Data journalism

Investigative journalists face growing legal, physical, psychological, and institutional pressures that shape how investigations are conducted. While prior research has documented risks to journalists, little empirical work has examined how different threats reconfigure investigative methods, particularly in Kazakhstan. This study addresses this gap through semi-structured interviews with 13 investigative journalists. The findings show that risk does not lead to the abandonment of investigative practices but to method-specific adaptations. Legal threats encourage the use of legally defensible approaches such as open-source research, official documents, data journalism, and collaboration, while discouraging anonymous sources and undercover work. Physical threats shift investigations toward remote and digitally mediated practices. Psychological pressure favors emotionally sustainable, analytical methods, and structural barriers limit access to official information, prompting reliance on independent data reconstruction and verification. By linking specific threats to distinct methodological responses, the study offers an empirically grounded framework for understanding how risk reshapes investigative journalism in Kazakhstan.

item.title: Facebook Community Standards: The New Gatekeeper for Palestinian News Organizations?
item.dc:creator: Nida’a Bassoumi, Naheda Mohammad Makhadmeh, Brian J. Bowe
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Nida’a Bassoumi, Naheda Mohammad Makhadmeh, Brian J. Bowe

Topics: Platform governance, Content moderation, News organizations, Social media platforms

This study examines how Facebook’s Community Standards act as a “gatekeeper” in ways that shape the editorial practices of Palestinian news organizations. It investigates how Facebook’s policies and algorithms influence their coverage of Palestine and the Israeli occupation. Findings reveal that these organizations navigate platform censorship by altering content and turning to platforms like Telegram to avoid restrictions, highlighting the tension between freedom of speech and maintaining visibility under digital constraints.

item.title: What Facebook Users Flag as False News: A Mixed-Methods Investigation of User-Reported Links
item.dc:creator: Anton Elias Holt
item.description:
Digital Journalism · Anton Elias Holt

Topics: Fake news, Platform governance, Political polarization, Content moderation

In January 2025 Meta announced the discontinuation of professional fact-checking on Facebook in the US, replacing fact-checkers with a Community Notes system, while simultaneously placing larger emphasis on user-reports for moderation. As earlier research has shown how user-reporting systems can be used strategically to silence opposing political views and minority voices, this raises new questions about how content on Facebook will change as a result of the decision. With a focus specifically on links rather than posts, this article speaks to the ongoing debate on user-driven moderation and Facebook’s 2025 policy change from a distinctive angle. Applying a mixed methods design, the article investigates links that have been reported as “False News” by users, providing a unique insight into an often opaque aspect of platform moderation. To guide the analysis, the article focuses on two critical cases: The 2018 election in Brazil, and links from the BBC.com domain. Results show that users generally report URLs with information about polarized political topics, indicating that users are not necessarily reporting content they think is false, but rather content they disagree with.

item.title: Receiving Online Support Matters: Disentangling the Effects of Seeking vs. Receiving Support on Social Media on Mental Health Under Stress
item.dc:creator: Rebekka Kreling
item.description:
Media Psychology · Rebekka Kreling

Topics: Social support, Social media use, Mental health, Well-being

Social media provide many opportunities to seek and receive support from close or distant others. Hopes of increased mental health by obtaining social support in an instant through social media have, however, been dimmed by inconsistent findings on the effect of online support on mental health and well-being. In a measurement burst diary study among university students in Germany featuring t = 6371 observations from n = 597 individuals, this paper highlights how relationships between online support and mental health are shaped by different steps within everyday supportive interactions: While seeking support is negatively related to mental health outcomes, receiving support via social media positively impacts mental health. The positive associations of receiving support and mental health were consistent in both multilevel regressions and random intercept cross-lagged panel models on the same and the next day. The context or intensity of stressors did not affect this relationship. Stressor intensity and context may, however, determine whether support needs are met in the online realm: Received support was lower when seeking online support for stressors with high intensity or in the context of friendships.

item.title: Assessing Civic Journalism Training: A Mixed-Method Applied Research Study
item.dc:creator: Joshua Darr, Susan Robinson
item.description:
Political Communication · Joshua Darr, Susan Robinson

Topics: Journalism, News framing, Audience engagement, Journalism education

This mixed‑method applied research study examines how audiences are responding to news stories that are shaped by retraining efforts to help American journalists rebuild audiences. We wanted to know: were these trainings working? Do audiences choose stories that were influenced by these trainings over more traditional elite-focused, problem-oriented, conflict-driven stories? Working with three newsroom-training organizations, we report the results of a series of conjoint experiments that test how well stories abiding by new journalistic techniques of engagement, solutions and “good-conflict” framing play with audiences. We then use the findings from seven focus groups (n = 49) with surveys to explain why people may have responded the way they did in the tests. We found that audiences overwhelmingly selected and appreciated the re-framed content and reported that it makes them trust the news brands more. The focus group participants claimed such content would entice them to become members, subscribe, or even donate to the mainstream brand – if they came across it. However, only a few of the participants said they had heard about the news outlet. Though the principles behind these trainings may seem counterintuitive to some journalists, they offer a potential path forward in uncertain times for local news.

item.title: Under Construction: Democracy Reporting as Paradigm Repair
item.dc:creator: Karin Assmann, Andrea Lorenz
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Karin Assmann, Andrea Lorenz

Topics: Journalistic roles, Press freedom, Democratic discourse, News organizations

In recent years, several news organizations in the United States have added a new beat to their newsrooms: the democracy beat. In this study, we analyze the metajournalistic discourse about the creation of teams tasked with democracy-specific reporting. We contribute to scholarship about the relationship between democracy and journalism at a time when both are under duress. The creation of democracy beats, we find, is a critique of political reporting as usual and an exercise in both paradigm repair and paradigm renewal. News outlets are trying to rehabilitate the normative role of journalists as watchdogs and defenders of democracy. Democracy desks are expected to adopt a more adversarial approach and critical standpoint as they challenge the objectivity paradigm. This study provides valuable insights into the institutional response of U.S. news organizations at the local, state, and national levels to attacks on the free press and to the escalating anti-media rhetoric putting journalism’s institutional role in a democratic society to the test.

item.title: Growing Inequalities Through Motivations: A Moderated Mediation Analysis Between Socioeconomic Status, Political Interest and News Media Consumption in Sweden, 1990–2023
item.dc:creator: Erik Espeland
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Erik Espeland

Topics: News consumption, Political interest, Socioeconomic status, Media use

As we have transitioned toward media systems increasingly characterized by proliferation of media choices, public and scholarly concern regarding widening news consumption gaps have grown. Two types of gaps have been especially prominent in research on news audience fragmentation. The first is research building on the opportunity, motivation and abilities (OMA) framework, showing that individual motivations and preferences are becoming more important when it comes to news consumption. The second is research focused on how high-choice media environments might contribute to socioeconomic (SES) gaps in news consumption. We know from previous research that these two gaps are related since SES shapes political interest through socialization processes, which in turn drives news consumption. However, previous research lacks an integrated longitudinal perspective, testing whether this mediated relationship has increased over time. Addressing these shortcomings, we utilize 33 years of Swedish survey data (NRespondents = 47 884) to conduct a moderated mediation analysis, simultaneously studying the direct effect of socioeconomic status as well as its indirect – mediated through political interest – effect on news consumption. Results suggest that socioeconomic gaps in news consumption have grown and that an important driver of these differences might be due to an increasing indirect effect through political interest.

item.title: A media ecology of hyperlocal resistance-the Indian farmers’ movement
item.dc:creator: Vineeta Dwivedi, Sunny Vijay Arora, Varun Nagaraj
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Vineeta Dwivedi, Sunny Vijay Arora, Varun Nagaraj

Topics: Alternative media, Political participation, Media trust, Digital activism

This article examines how protestors navigated a collapsing media environment during the Indian farmers’ movement of 2020–2021, one of the largest and most sustained protests in the country’s democratic history. Triggered by the passage of controversial agricultural marketing laws, the movement quickly became a site of contestation not only over economic reform but also over the legitimacy and role of the media. Legacy news media, widely perceived as aligning with government narratives, lost the trust of the protesting public. This study applies a media ecology framework, integrating McLuhan’s tetrad of media effects, and uses hermeneutic phenomenology to analyse the communicative dynamics of the protest movement. Drawing on interviews with protestors, union leaders, and journalists, as well as hyperlocal news artefacts and supported by field observations and media contextualisation, the study identifies three key dynamics: the breakdown of trust in institutional media, the emergence of decentralised hyperlocal channels, and the formation of insular communicative loops. Positioning McLuhan’s tetrad as an analytical extension within media ecology, this study empirically shows a crucial dimension of protest communication. While hyperlocal media enhance coordination, they also have the potential to be reversed into information loops. By mapping this paradox, the study advances Media Ecology Theory, enriches protest communication scholarship, and underscores the democratic risks arising from the loss of trust in traditional media.

item.title: Hyper-scaling from the cloud to the tower: platform enclosure and GenAI capture in higher education
item.dc:creator: Amelia Acker, Britt S. Paris
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Amelia Acker, Britt S. Paris

Topics: Platform governance, Artificial intelligence in higher education, Platformization, Digital infrastructure

The recent adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) platform services in higher education is notable not just for its speed of implementation but for how it is reshaping academic activities on campuses that are often slow to change. This article examines how cloud computing platforms are impacting knowledge production practices and scholarly infrastructure in US research universities through an analysis of academic cloud storage policy updates, AI feature rollouts, and institutional responses to AI service adoption. Drawing on critical university studies and critical informatics perspectives, we argue that cloud providers' functional sovereignty over academic data infrastructure is reshaping how universities produce, store, and share knowledge with platforms. Through critical case studies of major research universities' responses to Google Workspace's storage policy changes and Microsoft's Copilot expanding AI integration in campus enterprise software offerings, we demonstrate how cloud providers leverage scaling strategies, network effects, and institutional dependencies to extend their control over knowledge production and higher education. Our analysis shows how cloud infrastructure reinforces the neoliberal university's reliance on corporate computing systems, now subject to forces of hyper-scaling. As universities increasingly adopt AI tools for data-driven research and teaching methods, their dependence on commercial cloud services and big tech platforms deepens, strengthening firms' ability to exercise power through control of information infrastructure.

item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Kyle Beadle, Enrico Mariconti, Leonie Maria Tanczer, Marie Vasek

item.title: Reclaiming Place Through Symbolic Geographies: Visual Resistance on Palestinian Instagram
item.dc:creator: Insyirah Mujtahid, Nurul Huda Rashid, Kokil Jaidka
item.description:
Political Communication · Insyirah Mujtahid, Nurul Huda Rashid, Kokil Jaidka

Topics: Social media, Instagram, Visual communication, Alternative media

Palestinians use Instagram to construct symbolic geographies that resist displacement and assert cultural presence. Analyzing 9,126 posts from 834 users posted between October 2023-March 2024, we identify three recurring visual themes that serve as anchors of digital placemaking. The sharing of images depicting everyday routines and familiar spaces functions as an act of asserting belonging in the face of cartographic erasure. Resilience is conveyed through motifs of joy, family, and faith, symbolizing continuity under siege. Knowledge cultivation emerges through practices of naming places, traditions, and environmental markers, reinforcing cultural memory. Comparing Instagram content with 7,448 international news headlines, we find that user-generated posts often offer alternative framings that are absent in mainstream narratives. We close with a discussion of how Palestinian Instagram users created a networked archive that resists material destruction and algorithmic suppression, mapping threatened spaces and producing narrative coherence through everyday digital acts of documentation and resistance.

item.title: Enemies Abroad, Animosity at Home: Media Influence on U.S.-China Policy and Anti-Asian Sentiment
item.dc:creator: Siyu Liang
item.description:
Political Communication · Siyu Liang

Topics: Media framing, Media effects, Public opinion, News coverage

How do portrayals of foreign nations as threats shape public opinion on foreign policy and domestic racial attitudes? This study examines how portrayals of China as a threat influence Americans’ support for U.S. policy toward China and attitudes toward Asian Americans. A content analysis of CNN and Fox News transcripts from 2010 to 2020 shows that both outlets increasingly portrayed China as a threat, although Fox News more often emphasized threats to the United States, whereas CNN focused more on threats affecting other countries, international institutions, and populations. A national survey and a preregistered survey experiment further demonstrate that exposure to China threat narratives, regardless of whether the threat targets the United States or another country, increases support for hawkish U.S. foreign policy and heightens anti-Asian resentment, especially among Republicans. These findings show how portrayals of foreign threats shape public opinion and spill over into racial attitudes at home.

item.title: Where digital hate finds its home: perpetrators' preferred affordances and their experiences with content moderation and user intervention
item.dc:creator: Giang-Truong Nguyen, Stephanie Bührer, Kevin Koban, Jörg Matthes
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Giang-Truong Nguyen, Stephanie Bührer, Kevin Koban, Jörg Matthes

Topics: Digital hate, Social media affordances, Content moderation, Online harassment

Digital hate poses a significant challenge to democratic principles. However, not much is known about who produces it regularly, let alone across platforms. Drawing from routine activity theory as an overarching framework, our study investigated how the perceived importance of social media affordances is related to regular digital hate perpetrators’ platform use. Further, it explored how this usage is linked to experiences of moderation and interventions against them. Findings of quota-based surveys in four European countries (i.e., Austria, France, Hungary, and Sweden) suggest that perpetrators’ perceived importance of persistence and anonymity is consistently related to social media use across platforms, from which, in turn, primarily Telegram, Reddit, Twitch, and TikTok were linked to more frequent moderation and intervention experiences. By and large, our findings contribute to the current fight against digital hate by highlighting the need for regulatory strategies that account for perpetrators’ perceptions of affordances across platforms.

item.title: Affective Legitimacy and Digital Populism: Evidence from Romania’s Annulled Presidential Elections
item.dc:creator: Antonio Amuza, Vasile Dîncu
item.description:
Political Communication · Antonio Amuza, Vasile Dîncu

Topics: Populism, Digital media, TikTok, Political trust

On 6 December 2024, Romania’s Constitutional Court annulled the first round of presidential elections, triggering an exceptional crisis of democratic legitimacy in post-communist Europe. While procedurally justified, the decision sparked intense public reactions, both emotional and political. The findings confirm that populist interpretations of institutional actions proliferate in fragmented and emotionalized digital media environments, where distrust is personalized and intensified. Drawing on a nationally representative survey (N = 964), conducted by IRES shortly after the annulment, the study examines how Romanian citizens perceived the legitimacy of the Court’s decision and identifies the key socio-political and media-related factors shaping these perceptions. Binary logistic regression and mediation models were used to assess the drivers of perceived illegitimacy. TikTok use, negative emotions (anger, disappointment, resentment), political distrust, and anti-establishment party support significantly increase the likelihood of viewing the decision as illegitimate, whereas trust in journalists reduces it. The study contributes to the literature on populism as a communicative style and emotional register, showing how legitimacy itself becomes a contested symbol in digital environments marked by personalization, fragmentation, and affective intensification. We argue that institutional legitimacy is no longer grounded solely in procedural legality but is increasingly shaped by emotionally resonant narratives circulating through digital platforms. We complement the survey with a headline-level media analysis (N = 3,923; Dec 2024 - Aug 2025), to serve as a contextual counterfactual: instead of escalating antagonism, mainstream media gradually stabilize institutional language. A keyness comparison shows that the Early window (first 14 days) is driven by institutional/legal terms (CCR, decision, annulment), while the Late window becomes actor-centric (Simion, Antonescu, Ponta, Bolojan). Over time, lexical entropy declines markedly, signaling a standardization of vocabulary around procedural frames rather than escalating antagonism. Taken together, the results point to a decoupling between media normalization and individual affect, suggesting that democratic legitimacy in platformized communication environments is increasingly produced through affective legitimacy rather than procedural authority.

item.title: Entertainment as Trojan Horse: Voluntary Consumption of Propaganda in China
item.dc:creator: Hanzhang Liu, Linan Yao
item.description:
Political Communication · Hanzhang Liu, Linan Yao

Topics: Propaganda, Entertainment, Authoritarian media, Media effects

For authoritarian propaganda to change hearts and minds, it must first reach the masses and capture their attention. In an era of media proliferation, what can an authoritarian regime do to make ordinary citizens consume pro-regime propaganda voluntarily? How can it lower citizens’ resistance to being indoctrinated? In this article, we answer these questions by studying a new generation of propaganda movies in contemporary China. Leveraging observational data and a pre-registered survey experiment, we find that entertainment elements in propaganda movies – both personality-based and narrative-based – play a key role in appealing to viewers and increasing consumption; this effect is especially pronounced among groups that are the least inclined to expose themselves to propaganda in the first place. Also, viewers are more receptive to political indoctrination when it is interwoven with entertainment, even when they recognize such content. Combined, these findings highlight the importance of entertainment in authoritarian propaganda: not only does it serve as a vehicle to disseminate political indoctrination, but it also functions as a source of appeal that renders such indoctrination more palatable to the masses.
